We compared the conventional approach providing a single earliest estimated epidemic onset (EEEO) date for an entire field with an automated pixel-wise episensing workflow. To generate spatially explicit prognosis dates, we integrated a radiative transfer model with the CLS model, comparing uncrewed aerial systems (UAS) and Sentinel-2 (S2) imagery for estimating LAI and determining canopy closure dates. A General Additive Model confirmed that thecercospoRapackage successfully performed negative prognosis 21 das (days after sowing) earlier (μ̂UAS= 135.2 das, SE = 1.3) than the observed epidemic onset (μ̂observed= 156.9 das, SE = 0.4). Spatial analysis revealed greater variability in predicted onset dates from higher resolution remote sensing products (SDUAS= 12.5) compared to low resolution products (SDS2= 8.8). These results demonstrate that an episensing approach provide higher precision and automation capacity to provide greater spatial context by applying models at the pixel level, revealing spatial variability that classic field-scale or regional prognosis cannot resolve. Future improvements should consider additional variables and inoculum pressure for more precise epidemic onset definitions, alongside development of spatially explicit reference data.

title: 90.Developing a generic DSS model metadata catalogue and APIs for crop protection.
abstract: Decision Support Systems (DSS) in crop protection can give a helpful pest risk prognosis or recommendations for pest control, allowing farmers to make better-informed decisions. As a part of European Union policy strategy steering at the sustainable use of plant protection products, the EU H2020 project "IPM Decisions" created an online platform allowing farmers and advisors to access many DSS for major pests, weeds, and diseases in a variety of crops across Europe. The project has assessed and analyzed a set of research verified DSS's for integrated pest management. Information on the models employed by these DSS has been collected into a model catalogue, which is used by the IPM Decisions platform. Two Application Programming Interfaces (APIs) have been built to facilitate use of these models. In the spirit of the FAIR (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reproducible) principles, the DSS API provides access to DSS models with their metadata, including the description of model input and output parameters. Weather API allows access to European on-line weather data sources and adapts their offering to the needs of the DSS models. The new APIs work as part of the IPM Decisions Platform, but they are publicly available so that also other agricultural software such as crop protection applications or farm management information systems (FMIS) can use them. In this article, we discuss the development of DSS and Weather APIs and present their structures and definitions. Finally, we present the services that DSS API and Weather API provide, and demonstrate the use of the APIs in three application cases.

title: 91.VITA: variational pretraining of transformers for climate-robust crop yield forecasting.
abstract: Accurate crop yield forecasting is essential for global food security. However, current AI models systematically under-perform when yields deviate from historical trends. This issue arises from key data challenges, including a major asymmetry between rich pretraining weather datasets and the limited data available for fine-tuning. We introduceVITA (Variational Inference Transformer for Asymmetric data), a variational pretraining framework that addresses this asymmetry. Instead of relying on input reconstruction, VITA uses detailed weather variables as proxy targets during pretraining and learns to predict rich atmospheric states through self-supervised feature masking. This allows the model to be fine-tuned using only basic weather statistics during deployment. Applied to 763 counties in the U.S. Corn Belt, VITA achieves state-of-the-art performance in predicting corn and soybean yields across all evaluation scenarios. While it consistently delivers superior performance under normal conditions, its advantages are particularly pronounced during extreme weather years, with statistically significant improvements (paired t-test, p ≈ 0.01). Importantly, VITA outperforms prior frameworks like GNN-RNN using less data, making it more practical for real-world use-particularly in data-scarce regions. This work highlights how domain-aware AI design can overcome data limitations and support resilient agricultural forecasting in a changing climate.

title: 92.Hybrid statistical-machine learning approach for analyzing legacy and new phosphorus losses from subsurface drainage systems.
abstract: Phosphorus (P) is essential for crop growth but leaches through subsurface drainage discharge, impacting water quality. This study's objectives are: (1) apply machine learning to quantify the contributions of incidental (new) and legacy (old) P in drainage discharge from an Organic CL site (primarily organic fertilizers) and an Inorganic BL site (inorganic fertilizers), and (2) evaluate the effect of manure application timing on P loss. We collected data from two on-farm sites in southeast Michigan, USA. We applied the Weighted Regression on Discharge and Seasons (WRDS) equation to analyze P load based on drainage discharge and fertilizer application timing. The data were divided into calibration and validation sets, and a machine learning algorithm was employed for training. The results showed strong model prediction performance. Organic phosphorus sources contributed 2-4 times more to new P loss than inorganic sources. When applied during winter months (Dec and Jan), organic fertilizer contributed to greater new P loss, whereas early fall applications (Oct and Nov) resulted in lower new P loss, showing the importance of application timing. At the Organic CL site, legacy P was the dominant contributor to total phosphorus (TP) and dissolved reactive phosphorus (DRP) losses, accounting for 84% and 79% of losses, respectively. At the Inorganic BL site, legacy P was responsible for 97% of TP loss and the entirety (100%) of DRP loss. In conclusion, legacy P was the dominant source of P loss through drainage discharge, and timing of organic fertilizer application significantly influenced new P loss.

title: 93.Evaluation of morphological and biochemical properties of experimental pepper hybrids (Capsicum annuum L.) obtained by crossing with sterile (ms) lines.
abstract: The method of hybridization of sterilemslines with pure lines enabled the creation of F1 hybrids with pronounced heterosis effects in terms of fruit weight, number of fruits per plant, dry matter content and total sugars in a two-year study. Nine experimental pepper hybrids from three groups (LDCxHM6, LDCxHM5, LDCxHM4). Hybrid 6 (LDC6xHM5) has the highest average fruit weight (129.77 g), while hybrid 1 (LDC1xHM6) achieved the highest number of fruits per plant (27.33). The length of the fruit is relatively stable, while the thickness of the pericarp varies, with the highest value (5.13 mm) in hybrid 8 (LDC2xHM4). Hybrid 1 has the highest percentage of dry matter (10.80%) and content of total sugars (8.0 Brix). The research results indicate the potential of hybrids 1 and 6 for high yields and fruit quality, which makes them suitable for further selection in pepper breeding programs and hybrid 8 for processing.

title: 94.Leveraging Google Earth Engine for paddy field segmentation: a remote sensing and deep learning approach.
abstract: Precise segmentation of paddy fields using remote sensing is vital for advancing agricultural monitoring and optimizing resource allocation in precision farming. This study harnessed Google Earth Engine (GEE) and Sentinel-2 imagery to delineate paddy fields using the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and Land Surface Water Index (LSWI). A U-Net-based deep learning model, trained on 2000 labeled images, achieved a segmentation accuracy of 91%. This model was integrated into a mobile application to enable real-time and accessible monitoring by farmers and policymakers. This study details the dataset preparation, image preprocessing, segmentation methodology, model implementation, and practical deployment, offering a scalable solution for agricultural management in India and beyond.

title: 95.Macroeconomic determinants of food security in Ghana.
abstract: Hunger remains a persistent development challenge in sub-Saharan Africa, and Ghana is no exception despite decades of policy interventions and economic growth. This study investigates the macroeconomic determinants of food security in Ghana over the period 2001-2022, focusing on the roles of public agricultural employment, agricultural expenditure, and food inflation. Using ordinary least squares regression with a robust standard error, the study addresses potential heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation, ensuring robust inference. The results show that increased government spending on agriculture significantly reduces hunger rates, supporting the view that targeted investments in rural productivity and infrastructure are critical for sustainable food security. In contrast, a higher share of employment in agriculture is associated with increased hunger, highlighting the structural weakness of low-productivity subsistence farming and underscoring the need for rural economic transformation. Additionally, food inflation exerts a significant positive effect on hunger, demonstrating how rising food prices erode household purchasing power and worsen food insecurity. These findings align with the Structural Transformation Theory and recent empirical evidence. The study recommends scaling up effective agricultural investments, modernizing the agricultural workforce to enhance productivity, and implementing stronger food price stabilization measures to accelerate progress toward achieving Zero Hunger in Ghana.

title: 96.Sustainable maize yield optimization through subsurface drip irrigation, seeding, and nitrogen rate strategies in mid-Atlantic United States.
abstract: With the global population projected to reach 11.2 billion by 2100, enhancing maize yields through efficient irrigation and nutrient management is crucial for reducing yield gaps and ensuring food security. Subsurface drip irrigation (SDI) offers a promising alternative to traditional, less efficient methods. This three-year study (2022-2024) employed a split-split-plot design to evaluate optimal SDI strategies, including six dripline spacings (0.91-meter dripline, 1.82-meter dripline, 0.91-meter + volumetric water content (VWC) sensor, 0.91-meter + fertigation, 1.82-meter + fertigation (2022), 0.91-meter + Pivot Bio® (2023 and 2024), and non-irrigated (control)), four seeding rates (59,280 to 103,740 plants ha-1), and four nitrogen (N) rates (133 to 333 kg N ha-1). Data analysis revealed significant irrigation, N application, and seeding rates on grain yield, and irrigation by N rates interactions each year. Yearly irrigation impact on yield was 102%, 13%, and 51% over non-irrigated in 2022, 2023, and 2024, respectively. The 0.91- meter dripline averaged the greatest revenue ($985 ha-1) over non-irrigated. The 0.91- meter dripline + VWC Sensor showed the strongest relationship between N rates and grain yield in 2022 (R2= 0.997), while the 0.91-meter dripline + Pivot Bio had the greatest effect in 2023 (R2= 0.998) and 2024 (R2= 1.000). These findings highlight SDI's effectiveness in increasing maize yield and profitability, reducing production risks in Virginia and the Mid-Atlantic region. The study shows the potential of targeted irrigation and nutrient management to maximize maize yields.

title: 98.Performance of honeybee (Apis mellifera Linnaeus, 1758) colonies with dearth period pollen supplements.
abstract: Pollen supplements are artificial proteinaceous feed containing a minimum of 5 to 25 percent of actual pollen. The quality of the supplemental feed during dearth period (pollen and nectar scarcity) influences the development and strength of the honeybee,Apis melliferaLinnaeus, 1758 colonies. Plant based proteins such as pulses are researched as potential pollen supplements for the dearth periods. The experiment was performed at commercial apiary, the Sagar Honeybees located at Narayani river basin, Gaindakot-8, Nawalparasi East, Nepal from June to December 2023 to examine their feed preferences and the effect of various pulses on brood area, pollen and nectar storage area, number of bee combs per colony and honey production across honeybee hives. The treatments we used are local beekeepers' choices which they are using as homemade artificial feeds and empirically claim differential impacts on bee colonies. Twenty healthy honeybee colonies were supplied with four pulse-based pollen supplement patties (treatments) each constituting either of soybean (Glycine max), black gram (Vigna mungo), chickpea (Cicer arietinum), and pea (Pisum sativum), and a control treatment comprised sugar syrup solution (1 liter/week/hive) and each treatment replicated four times in bee hives on top of brood chamber. Among the pollen supplemented pulse patties, the mean consumption per week of black gram patties was higher (98.72 g) than soybean (89.73 g), chickpea (82.44 g) and pea (77.18 g). However, the maximum capped area was observed in soybean-based pollen supplements (1257.84 ± 18.92 cm2) and minimum in control (560.95 ± 37.22 cm2). Similarly, maximum uncapped area, pollen area, nectar area, honeybee combs covered with bees was observed in colonies fed with soybean-based pollen supplement patties followed by black gram, chickpea and pea while the minimum was detected in the control. The maximum honey yield was observed in soybean-based pollen supplement fed hives (12.20 kg) and minimum in control hives (6.09 kg). The results clearly showed that supplementary feeding increased honeybee colony strength and honey production and among them, soybean-based pollen supplement fed hives showed better yield attributing factors indicating sustained brood production and honeybee population build-up during the dearth period.

title: 99.Modelling the impact of reporting rates on outbreak detection with implications for managing emergency animal diseases.
abstract: The detection and surveillance of emergency animal disease outbreaks play a crucial role in their management. However, monitoring such diseases can often rely on farmers self-reporting animal infection. If there are disincentives for farmers to report disease, this can lead to delayed reporting, which can negatively impact outbreak management outcomes. To understand how farmer reporting rates impact the outcomes of outbreak management strategies, we model the spread of animal disease using an agent-based model. We investigate how varying the reporting rate for infected properties can impact firstly the total number of properties depopulated for various management strategies and secondly which strategy is optimal. Our model considers disease transmission occurring both within a property, through animal-to-animal transmission, and between properties, through wind dispersal of fomites and random movement of animals. Using this model, we compare the number of properties depopulated under four strategies: depopulating infected properties and animal movement restrictions combined with (1) ring culling, (2) ring testing, (3) ring vaccination (with a perfect vaccine), and (4) ring vaccination (with an imperfect vaccine). Given our assumptions and model structure, we find that outbreaks spread in clusters around an initially infected property, with additional clusters being seeded early by the random movement of animals between properties. We simulate the impact of reporting rates on a range of outbreak indicators, and we find it has the biggest impact on the time to detection. This time decreases as we increase the reporting rate, but with diminishing returns. We find the timing of outbreak detection impacts the total properties depopulated under all management strategies similarly, as outbreaks detected earlier ultimately lead to smaller outbreaks. As such, we find that varying the reporting rate had minimal impact on which strategy was optimal for a given simulation. Our modelling demonstrates how human behaviour, such as reporting rates, can impact the outcomes from managing emergency animal disease outbreaks. While exact behaviour cannot be predicted for future outbreaks, we can prepare for the next outbreak of emergency animal disease by investigating which management strategies can be robust to a variety of human behaviours.

title: 100.Análisis morfogenético de aislamientos de Cercospora kikuchii provenientes de distintas regiones de la Argentina.
101.Scalable methods for quantifying the stay green ability of corn for yield prediction by using satellite image.
abstract: Recent advancements in unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and satellite imagery have the potential to reshape plot-level evaluation of crop varieties, a key process in agricultural research. This study evaluated the potential of Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) data, derived from satellite imagery, to assess the yield of four row maize test plots across four locations with varying nitrogen treatments. We determined that the area under a polynomial curve fit to NDVI-GDD (growing degree days) can function as an effective predictor of yield. This metric, derived from satellite imagery, demonstrated strong correlations with direct measurements of yield both within individual environments and across all locations (r = 0.83), with within-environment correlation coefficients with yield ranging from 0.45 to 0.72. This study provides a foundation for scalable, efficient, and physiologically informed remote yield estimation across diverse environments.

title: 102.Pythium-induced changes in bacterial and fungal community structure in hydroponically grown lettuce.
abstract: The composition and structure of plant-associated microbial communities are shaped by both abiotic and biotic factors, with host-related traits and plant-microbe interactions playing key roles. While studies on soil-based cultivation systems have shown that pathogen infection can disrupt plant microbial communities, little is known about how pathogen interactions affect hydroponically grown crops, particularly leafy greens. Despite the controlled conditions of hydroponic cultivation, these systems remain vulnerable to waterborne pathogens likePythiumspp. These oomycetes can rapidly spread through recirculated nutrient solutions and cause severe root diseases. This study aimed to examine howPythium aphanidermatuminoculation affects the bacterial and fungal communities of hydroponic lettuce under research greenhouse conditions. Our findings indicated that root inoculation withP. aphanidermatumsignificantly impacted lettuce biomass. Moreover, the bacterial community structure and composition in inoculated roots differed significantly from non-inoculated controls, regardless of disease severity (low and high). In contrast, no significant shifts were observed in fungal community structure. Differential abundance and network analyses identified Pseudomonas andOlpidiumas consistently associated withPythium-inoculated roots. The shifts in microbial composition and structure followingPythiuminoculation may indicate dysbiosis and point towards taxa that need to be further explored. A deeper understanding of hydroponics-associated microbial communities, their interactions, and functional roles will allow us to leverage these relationships for improved food security and environmental sustainability. Moreover, understanding the microbial composition dynamics during pathogen infection can have significant implications for disease management and the effective use of biological control agents.

title: 103.Improved quality control and moisture determination in dry kava (Piper methysticum) from Vanuatu: a practical oven-drying approach.
abstract: Dry kava (Piper methysticum) exports in the Pacific Island region are booming, and quality control remains a critical factor affecting the reputation of exports in the global market. This study evaluates trends in the quality of dry kava in Vanuatu, determines a practical AOAC oven-drying method for moisture analysis, and assesses the effects of drying on kava chemo-type and colorimetric absorbance. A national database of colorimetric absorbance measurements from 2016 to 2024 was analysed, using the benchmark that high-quality "noble" kava has an absorbance value lower than 0.84 ± 0.05, according to previous studies. For moisture determination, samples were dried at 105°C in an oven for 0.5, 1, 1.5, and 2 hours and compared against the Infrared (IR) thermal combustion method, with further verification by FTIR spectral analysis. Results indicate that kava quality in Vanuatu has significantly improved from 2016 to 2024, with absorbance values dropping from 0.72 to 0.48, reflecting enhanced quality control measures across the export value chain. The 2-hour oven drying method showed high agreement with the IR method (R2= 0.99, Bias = 0.12, Precision = 0.2, RMSE = 0.20), better repeatability (SD = 0.03, RSD = 0.22%), and strong reproducibility (SD = 0.04, RSD = 0.29%). Limits of agreement fell within a narrow range (±0.25%). The method also showed strong linearity (R2= 0.99) and low variation based on chemo-type selectivity and specificity based on principal component analysis of FTIR spectra of dry kava. The FTIR qualitative results also revealed a breakdown of polar compounds, particularly carbohydrates and sugars, at 1050 cm-1, along with notable changes at 1640, 1740, and 2920 cm-1, indicating loss of volatile esters, lipid oxidation, and residual moisture after 4 hours of drying. Regarding drying temperature, samples reached constant weight after 4 hours drying time at 125°C to 131°C (difference of 0.004%), and showed significant difference compared to drying at 105°C for the same duration. A significant correlation (p ≤ 0.05) was also observed between colorimetric absorbance and weight loss in a narrow margin, suggesting that future kava nobility assessments should correct for moisture content. These findings demonstrate that the 2-hour oven drying method at 105°C is a practical and reliable approach for routine moisture analysis in dry kava and can support improved quality control in the kava industry.

title: 104.Socio-economic determinants of safe pesticide use among vegetable growers in Jaipur District: a multivariate and machine learning analysis.
abstract: Vegetable production is a vital component of Rajasthan's agricultural economy, particularly in the Jaipur district. However, it faces significant challenges due to a wide range of biotic stresses. To mitigate these losses, the judicious and informed use of pesticides is essential. This study investigates the relationship between socio-economic variables and pesticide utilization behavior among vegetable growers. Bassi and Amber tehsils of the Jaipur district were purposively selected for their prominence in vegetable cultivation. From each tehsil, four villages were randomly chosen, and fifteen vegetable growers per village were selected and yielding a total sample of 120 respondents. Correlation analysis was conducted to examine the relationships between socio-economic factors and pesticide utilization behaviors. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was employed to model a latent construct of "pesticide utilization behavior," predicted by socio-economic variables, using maximum likelihood estimation with robust corrections for ordinal data. Additionally, a decision tree analysis was used to validate predictors of behavior. Findings revealed that crop diversity, measured by the number of crops grown, consistently emerged as a key determinant across all analytical methods. Farmers cultivating a greater variety of crops demonstrated higher pesticide utilization behaviors, potentially increasing health and environmental risks due to practices such as overuse, improper disposal, and unintended harm to pollinators. These results emphasize the importance of targeted interventions and educational strategies tailored to diverse cropping systems to promote safer pesticide use.

title: 105.Emerging viral threats to tomato in the Philippines: insights from high-throughput sequencing and molecular diagnostics of tomato leaf curl disease in Central Visayas and Southern Luzon.
abstract: Tomato is an economically and nutritionally important crop in the Philippines. However, it remains vulnerable to viral diseases, particularly tomato leaf curl disease (ToLCD). Despite the development of new varieties, the continuous emergence, recombination, and diversification of viruses pose significant challenges. Given the limited scope of viral surveillance in the country, this study aimed to gain insights into emerging viral threats to tomato through high-throughput sequencing (HTS) and molecular diagnostics of ToLCD-affected plants in Central Visayas (Cebu and Bohol) and Southern Luzon (Laguna), Philippines. HTS and molecular analyses revealed the presence of tomato yellow leaf curl Kanchanaburi virus (TYLCKaV), the first bipartite begomovirus infecting tomato in the Philippines, and a recombinant tobacco leaf curl Yunnan virus-Philippines strain (TbLCYNV-Ph), which carries a V2 gene (pre-coat protein) from tomato leaf curl Cebu virus (ToLCCeV). In addition to tomato, other solanaceous crops such as pepper (showing leaf curl symptoms in Cebu and Zamboanga) and eggplant (exhibiting yellow mosaic symptoms in Albay) were also found to be infected with TYLCKaV, indicating its broader host range and geographic distribution. Meanwhile, the tomato leaf curl Philippines virus (ToLCPV)-Laguna isolate HM, a variant of the previously reported recombinant ToLCPV-Laguna strain, exhibited a new recombination event in the right intergenic region, derived from ageratum enation virus (AEV). PCR-based validation confirmed the presence of all these viruses in symptomatic tomato field samples collected over multiple years. Additionally, a novel deltasatellite, provisionally designated as tomato leaf curl Philippines deltasatellite (ToLCPD), potentially associated with the ToLCPV-Laguna isolate HM, was assembled and redetected via PCR. The ageratum yellow vein Singapore alphasatellite (AYVSGA), potentially associated with the TbLCYNV-Ph strain, was also identified through HTS. These findings highlight the dynamic and evolving landscape of tomato viruses and subviral agents involved in ToLCD in the Philippines. The emergence of novel recombinants and new viral records emphasizes the need for continuous surveillance and molecular characterization. This HTS-based study on tomato viruses in the Philippines has direct implications for virus management and resistance breeding, contributing to a more resilient and sustainable tomato industry in the country.

title: 106.Participatory assessment of maize productivity following the transition from conventional ridge tillage to deep bed farming system in Malawi.
abstract: Climate change and soil degradation threaten agricultural productivity in Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), particularly in Malawi where smallholder farming systems predominate. This study presents a comparative assessment of deep bed farming (DBF) a hybrid conservation agriculture practice versus conventional ridging (CR) in smallholder maize-based farming systems through participatory on-farm quasi-experiments that positioned farmers as co-researchers. Across diverse agroecological zones, we implemented a randomized complete block design under farmer management to systematically evaluate both cultivation methods. DBF significantly (p ≤ 0.001) outperformed CR, supporting higher plant populations of 450 vs 350 maize plants per 10 m2(45,000 vs. 35,000 plants ha-1), higher stalk biomass yield of 75 vs. 50 kg per 10 m2(7,500 vs. 5,000 kg ha-1), and 70% greater grain yields (8.5-9.0 vs. 5.0 metric tonnes ha-1). These outcomes are attributed to DBF's enhancement of soil structure, moisture retention, and biological activity. The co-creation approach validated DBF's agronomic benefits while fostering local ownership, enabling real-time adaptation and enhancing adoption potential. Our findings highlight DBF as a scalable, climate-resilient practice capable of strengthening food security and ecological sustainability in resource-constrained smallholder systems.

title: 107.Soybean cyst nematode reproduction and soybean biomass: the legacy of soil cropping histories.
abstract: The soybean cyst nematode (SCN), Heterodera glycines, represents the most yield-limiting pathogen of soybean in North America. Although crop rotation serves as a common SCN management strategy, the influence of previous cropping history on nematode establishment in previously non-infested (naïve) soils remains poorly understood. This study examined the impact of various cropping histories on SCN establishment of naïve soils. We hypothesized that recent soybean cropping would leave a biochemical legacy, particularly through root exudates, that enhances SCN abundance by promoting egg hatching and infectivity, as measured by final egg counts after one full SCN life cycle. To test this, we conducted a series of greenhouse experiments using soil from fields with different cropping histories and no SCN infestation, including continuous soybean, rotational soybean, horticultural cropping, prairie, Kernza, and fallow fields. In general, cropping history had no impact on final SCN abundance. Similarly, susceptible soybean varieties did not interact with cropping history to influence SCN abundance. Cropping history also failed to consistently affect plant biomass after infestation. In three experiments, however, SCN infestation was associated with increased soybean biomass, potentially reflecting compensatory growth responses. These findings suggest that SCN establishment in naïve soils occurs largely independently of recent cropping history. Further research should target the mechanism underlying compensatory growth and their implications for soybean yield and nematode management strategies.

title: 108.Genetic and post-weaning diet interventions for enhancing pig growth rates, carcass yield, and quality.
abstract: Pig productivity is significantly affected by genetics and diet, so we determined the effects of pig genotype and post-weaning diet on their performance. Diets based on maize bran (MB), wheat bran (WB), and whole maize(WM) were fed to Cambrough (CC) (n=18,12.0 kg), Cambrough×LargeWhite (CL) crossbreds (n=18,9.6 kg) and Local Black (LB) (n=18,6.5 kg). Each genotype, sex of the pigs were randomly allocated to diets and fed for 120 days. Data collected: feed intake (FI), live weight (LWT), back-fat-thickness (BFT), and body-condition-score (BCS). At 180 days old, all males were slaughtered. Diet and genotype significantly influenced (P<0.05) growth and carcass characteristics. Weight gains were 360, 420, and 390 g/day for WM, MB, and WB; while the feed cost per kg of pork was US$1.13, 0.86, and 0.52, respectively. CC pigs had less back fat (4.8 mm) than crossbreds (7.7 mm) and tenderness score of 7.04 compared to 7.01 of CL pigs. Lean % was 33.5% (WM), 34.0% (MB), and 40.0% (WB) while acceptability scores by the trained panel were 6.45 (CC) and 6.42 (CL). WB diet was least-cost and produced better pig performance and pork quality than maize-based diets. CC pigs had leaner pork than CL. Bran should be the energy ingredient of choice in Uganda; Cambrough breed should be promoted among pig farmers in the Lake Victoria Crescent region.

title: 109.Virtual Agronomist - an AI-assisted chatbot for guiding crop management decisions of smallholder farmers in Africa.
abstract: African smallholder farmers' access to agronomic advice is limited by the small number of agricultural extension officers. Virtual Agronomist is designed as a scientifically sound, digital advisory system to provide farmers with tailored, actionable, and cost-effective advice for soil and crop management decisions throughout the season. The system aims to help farmers increase crop yields, profitability, and input-use efficiency, and improve soil health. It is delivered via WhatsApp, assisted by ChatGPT to aid communication. Upon registration, farmers are prompted to georeference their plots and verify the resulting polygons on a displayed map. A suggested target yield and nutrient management plan are generated from a model using soil property data downloaded from the iSDA soil property map of Africa and chatbot responses from farmers on soil and crop management history. Farmers are prompted throughout the season to make observations on crop emergence, weeds, pests, and diseases, and they receive tailored management advice based on simple rule models. A lead farmer dissemination model is used to overcome the limitations of smartphone penetration and language constraints, supported through an incentive payment scheme. The unique combination of big data, AI, and digital communication tools appears to enable fast uptake, with over 100,000 plots registered across several African countries and 4 million individual messages from farmers within a few months of its deployment. Within this same timeframe, an uptake penetration of 78% of farmers in one Kenyan county was achieved. Retrospective cohort surveys across countries and crops indicate a yield improvement of 1.4- to 1.9-fold compared to farmers not using the service. The marginal cost of delivering Virtual Agronomist is $1.50 USD per farmer per season, with a clear path to cost reduction at scale. The low cost of national-level deployment, the high percentage of farmers reached, and the intensity of within-season advice clearly outperform existing extension services.

title: 110.Multivariate clustering and decomposition of cereal production in Rajasthan: insights for agricultural policy.
abstract: Agriculture is the backbone of India, however, some state like Rajasthan has diverse conditions with potential for agricultural production. The present article has statistically evaluated the five major cereal crops, i.e., Jowar, Bajra, Maize, Wheat, and Barley. The analysis was based one time series data on area (thousand hectares), production (thousand tonnes), and yield (tonnes per hectare) for the above mentioned five crops from 1970-71 to 2023-24 and procured form the Bulletin of Agricultural Statistics, Govt. of Rajasthan and Directorate of Economics & Statistics, Government of India. The methodology is implemented using R (version 4.3.2) in RStudio. The preparation of data and cleaning of data have also been performed using this software. The application of multivariate time series clustering, decomposition of production changes, and cluster-specific decomposition analysis was used to meet the objectives of the research article. Finding reveals that the two clusters i.e., high-yield which has found stable and low-yield clusters, need differentiated policy approaches. Yield-driven growth in Cluster 1 demonstrates the success of irrigation and modern inputs, while Cluster 2's reliance on area expansion signals an opportunity for yield-enhancing innovations. The policy recommendations address these patterns, promoting sustainable productivity in a region critical to India's food security.

title: 111.A general formula for individualized profit-optimal livestock production.
abstract: Livestock producers face a critical economic challenge: determining the optimal time to sell animals as their growth efficiency diminishes with age. Here we integrate metabolic scaling theory with economic optimization to derive a general analytical formula for the optimal selling weight that maximizes profit for individual animals. This analysis also reveals a simple criterion to identify which animals will generate profit based on the relationship between current market conditions (feed costs relative to meat prices) and individual animal metabolic efficiency. Testing our framework on 378 Japanese Black cattle increased individual profits by 38 ± 21% over conventional rate-of-gain thresholds, requiring only three strategic weight measurements per animal. Our framework provides a theoretical foundation for practical livestock management that enhances both profitability and resource efficiency in agricultural systems.

title: 112.Landscape structure, climate variability, and soil quality shape crop biomass patterns in agricultural ecosystems of Bavaria.
abstract: Understanding how environmental variability shapes crop biomass is essential for improving yield stability and guiding climate-resilient agriculture. To shed more light on this relationship, biomass estimates derived from a semi-empirical light use efficiency (LUE) model are compared against those predicted using a machine learning-remote sensing approach that incorporates environmental variables. Specifically, we combined a light use efficiency (LUE) model with a random forest (RF) approach to predict the mean crop biomass across the years 2001-2019 for winter wheat (WW) and oilseed rape (OSR) across the entire region of Bavaria, Germany. Using a 5 km2hexagon-based spatial framework, we integrated LUE-derived biomass with spatial predictors - including the Shannon Diversity Index (SHDI) of land cover diversity, small woody features (SWF), elevation, slope angle, aspect, and soil potential - and spatio-temporal climate variables, specifically the seasonal (growing-season) mean and standard deviation (SD) of temperature, precipitation, and solar radiation from 2001 to 2019. The RF model, trained on LUE biomass and validated against district-level yields and test-set LUE data, outperformed the LUE model alone - achieving R2= 0.87 and RMSE = 2.85 dt ha-1for WW, and R2= 0.86 and RMSE = 1.24 dt ha-1for OSR, with particularly strong improvements for WW. Model interpretation using variable importance, SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP), and partial dependence plots (PDPs) revealed that WW biomass was primarily driven by landscape and topographic variables, while OSR was more sensitive to solar radiation and soil potential. For analytical purposes, Bavaria was divided into six agricultural regions. SHDI and SWF appeared to promote biomass production in Franconia and the Tertiary Hills Region, while topographic and climatic limitations were more pronounced in alpine and hill regions. Both crops showed biomass gains in landscapes where SHDI exceeded 0.80, indicating moderate to high land-cover diversity - and where SWF cover approached 7% of the hexagon area, suggesting benefits from moderate structural complexity. However, reductions in biomass were observed under high landscape variability, particularly in SHDI. Climatic thresholds differed between crops: WW biomass declined beyond a mean growing-season temperature of 21°C, while OSR declined beyond 12°C, reflecting crop-specific thermal tolerances. By combining the LUE model's mechanistic strengths with RF's flexible, non-linear learning capabilities, and incorporating spatial and temporal environmental conditions, this study presents a scalable framework for biomass prediction and analyzing factors influencing its variability in space. The findings provide valuable insights into region- and crop-specific environmental responses, supporting agri-environmental planning and land management under increasing climate variability.

title: 113.Removing wolves did not reliably prevent domestic animal losses.
abstract: Humans usually kill wild animals that they perceive as threats. However, many scientific findings have raised doubts that killing solves wildlife damage to property. With scant, low-quality data, uncertainty persists. We reviewed recent studies of killing gray wolves to protect domestic animals. Our inclusion criteria set a minimum threshold for robust study design and transparent data sharing. In five studies in five countries, Killing wolves typically had no effect, may have had the desired effect but more often wolf-killing had the counter8 productive undesirable effect of elevating domestic animal losses. We quantified the relative rates of the three outcomes and find the balance in favor of no effect to undesirable effects. We discuss potentially confounding variables and the need for an unbiased, reproducible, transparent randomized, and controlled trial of predator removal. We find and summarize similarities to other situations from disease transmission to crop damage.

title: 114.The benefits of an attractive companion: modelling non-persistently transmitted plant virus control via trap or repellent companion plants.
abstract: Non-persistently transmitted (NPT) plant viruses are a major threat to global food security, and are transmitted between plants by aphid vectors, acquired and inoculated through brief epidermal probes. This fast mode of transmission makes control of NPT viruses difficult. Companion plants - a secondary plant species intercropped with the main host - could be used for disease control. Two options are 'trap' and 'repellent' companions that, respectively, attract the aphid away from the main host or repel the aphid from the field. However, while explored for aphid pest control, their use has been scarcely explored for NPT virus control despite experimental evidence of their efficacy. Via a mechanistic mathematical model of NPT virus transmission, we show that both companion plant types can control NPT viruses. However, trap plants appear to be a more reliable method with more consistent control efficacy and yield benefits across a range of different model parameterisations. Repellent plants may be most useful in scenarios with highly mobile aphids migrating across an infected landscape. With less mobile aphids they can counter intuitively worsen an epidemic through increasing aphid movement, despite decreasing aphid numbers. We also show that virus manipulation of plant phenotype (in particular 'attract-and-deter'), which changes aphid behaviour to increase virus transmission, often reduces control efficacy, particularly for trap plants, but in certain circumstances can increase repellent plant control efficacy. Overall, we conclude that these companion plant types, rarely considered for NPT virus control, could be valuable tools.

title: 115.Sustainability of plant clinics for improved plant health systems.
abstract: Using qualitative methods, this study provides insights on the foundations upon which various recommendations from the literature for improving plant clinics in the global south are based and the practical challenges which test their field applicability. Findings reveal three broad, interlinked, thematic areas - capacity strengthening and stakeholder engagement, digitalisation and technology, and governance and planning. No single recommendation is a cure-all for the challenges that plague plant clinics, but when implemented coherently, the various recommendations have potential to improve plant clinic operations while concurrently strengthening national plant health systems. Policy makers and practitioners should ensure continuous upskilling on plant health of frontline extension agents, while leveraging digital technology and optimising public agricultural extension services. Furthermore, any actions to improve plant clinics must be implemented with a local lens - contextualising them to suit the prevailing socio-cultural context within which plant clinics operate. Future research should focus on ground truthing the various recommended actions to develop actionable solutions for policy makers and plant health practitioners.

title: 116.Abiotic stress mitigation by a novel plant biostimulant combining the benefits of glycine-betaine and vegetal derived protein hydrolysate on different crops under controlled conditions.
abstract: Abiotic stress factorssuch as drought, extreme temperatures, excessive moisture, and saline irrigation water can significantly reduce crop productivity and yields. These stressors often occur simultaneously - such as drought and heat - exacerbating their negative impact on yield and quality. Consequently, there is considerable interest in developing novel Plant Biostimulants (PB) to mitigate the effects of abiotic stress. A new PB was developed based on the synergistic effects of a plant protein hydrolysate and Glycine Betaine as observed in preliminary development trials. Investigating synergistic interactions between different biostimulants has been proposed as a promising strategy for creating more effective formulations. The biostimulant was tested under controlled conditions in growth chambers on young maize (Zea mays) plants under drought stress and on strawberry (Fragaria × ananassa) plants under frost stress. In repeated trials, the new formulation significantly mitigated the negative effects of both drought and frost stress, as evidenced by improved chlorophyll content, increased fresh biomass, and higher marketable strawberry yields. These results obtained under simulated stress conditions demonstrate the product's efficacy and suggest its potential as a valuable tool for mitigating abiotic stress in field applications.

title: 117.Genotype, environment and management effects on grain yield, milling quality, and nutritional density of oat in the Northern Great Plains
abstract: Markets demand grain characteristics that are consistent despite weather extremes and may be negatively correlated, such as between yield and nutritional value. Selecting crop varieties and management practices is important for meeting these market demands. We examined the impact of three genotypes, namely Reins, Natty, and Sumo across three growing environments (2021-2023), and two management practices that included three planting densities (low, recommended, and high) and two clover establishment practices (under-seeded clover with oats and fallow with no clover) on oat (Avena sativaL.) grain yield, milling quality, and nutritional content. Across 2021-2023, precipitation ranged from 176 to 328 mm and average daily maximum temperatures from 23.0 to 25.9°C. Cooler and wetter conditions generally supported higher yields and better milling quality, but at the cost of lower grain protein and β-glucan content. An average grain yield, test weight, protein content, and β-glucan content, and plump value across genotypes and treatments are 2906 kg ha-1, 43.1 kg hl-1, 4.72%, 18.6%, and 82.4%, respectively. Variety selection and management could mitigate weather impacts and tradeoffs among grain characteristics. The semi-dwarf variety, Reins excelled in favorable conditions, while medium-height Natty and Sumo tolerated drier conditions. Seeding rate also influenced grain nutrient content and milling quality, with higher populations resulting in higher test weight, kernel plumpness, oil, and protein content but lower thousand kernel weight. An additional, rotationally beneficial management practice, clover forage establishment, did not affect grain yield or quality. Tradeoffs among grain characteristics were variety-specific – Sumo best maintained milling quality and nutritional content irrespective of test weight, while Reins maintained grain quality traits across yield environments. To better meet the demands of the food oats market, breeders may further decouple grain quality traits while continuing to select for weather resilience. Agronomists, meanwhile, may revisit planting densities while continuing to develop soil-building practices.

title: 118.Tracking organic acids in chickpea root-exudates under different iron provisions towards biofortification through rhizosphere enrichment.
abstract: Micronutrient malnutrition, particularly iron deficiency, is a significant challenge in developing countries. Crop biofortification presents an innovative approach to enhance the nutritional value of crops, thereby combating this issue. The efficiency of iron (Fe) uptake, deposition, and accumulation is largely genotype-dependent, and root exudation of organic acids (OAs) plays a critical role in nutrient acquisition, disease resistance, and drought tolerance. This study investigates the effect of varying iron concentrations on the type and concentration of organic acids secreted in the root exudates of chickpea (Cicer arietinumL.), a promising legume for iron biofortification and anaemia alleviation in arid regions. Chickpea seeds were germinated in vitro on MS basal medium after surface sterilization. Plantlets were subsequently transferred to liquid MS media supplemented with different concentrations of Fe-EDTA: 0 (control), 1X (27.8 mg/L), 3X (83.4 mg/L), 5X (139 mg/L), and 10X (278 mg/L). Root exudates were collected, freeze-dried, and analyzed using Liquid Chromatography with Tandem Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to identify secreted OAs. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) was employed to quantify selected organic acids. No organic acids were detected in the 0 Fe-EDTA control medium. In contrast, several organic acids were secreted in response to low iron levels, including glycolic, butyric, pyruvic, oxalic, lactic, gluconic, propionic, and glyoxylic acids. At higher iron concentrations, malonic, oxalic, and lactic acids were produced. Notably, oxalic acid was identified as playing a substantial role in iron acquisition. Our findings demonstrate that organic acids significantly contribute to iron acquisition in chickpea. This research highlights the potential of utilizing organic acid secretion as a strategy for crop biofortification and enhancing mineral availability in the rhizosphere, paving the way for improved nutritional interventions in agriculture.

title: 119.RationSolverPy: a Python-based computational tool integrating linear programming and nutritional science for precision broiler feed formulation.
abstract: The imperative for precision in feed formulation is paramount for optimizing the economic performance, flock health, and environmental sustainability of broiler production systems. This paper introduces RationSolverPy, an open-source computational tool developed within the Python ecosystem, designed to address the complexities of least-cost broiler feed formulation through the application of linear programming (LP). While LP remains the established methodology, the distinct contribution of RationSolverPy lies in its provision of an accessible, adaptable, and transparent platform that integrates essential practical functionalities. These include user-configurable variable energy targets, explicit control over the calcium-to-phosphorus ratio, constraints on maximum dietary fat, a user-friendly graphical interface (GUI) for interaction, and a persistent calculation history mechanism. The underlying methodology leverages established avian nutritional requirements, exemplified herein using Ross 308 broiler specifications, coupled with a standard LP model solved utilizing the efficient 'highs' algorithm accessed via the scipy.optimize.linprog library function. This work provides a detailed exposition of the mathematical model underpinning the tool and elaborates on the software architecture and implementation specifics. Crucially, it presents a validation study wherein the tool's outputs are rigorously compared against a published benchmark formulation problem, thereby demonstrating its computational accuracy. Furthermore, the utility of its flexible features, such as the capacity for multi-level energy calculations, is illustrated. RationSolverPy represents a valuable, validated, non-commercial research prototype, offering researchers and nutritionists an efficient and customizable alternative to potentially less flexible or cost-prohibitive commercial software solutions for the development of precise broiler rations.

title: 120.Impact of COVID-19 pandemic on dairy farmers in Mandya district of Karnataka - an economic analysis.
abstract: The newly discovered corona virus (COVID-19), which was discovered for the first time on November 17, 2019, in Wuhan, China, ended up being a pandemic. The Indian government declared a statewide lockdown on March 24, 2020, lasting until May 31, 2020, as a preventative precaution against the pandemic. Every area of the Indian economy, including the dairy sector, has been impacted by these policies. Dairy farmers and dairy cooperatives are the most impacted dairy industry stakeholders. The current study was conducted to evaluate the financial effects of the COVID-19 epidemic on dairy producers and the dairy cooperative in the Karnataka district of Mandya. The pre-lockdown, lockdown, and post-lockdown phases were all included in the study. A study was conducted on one milk union and 100 dairy farmers. Analytic tools such trend analysis, wilcoxon signed rank test, quantity gap analysis and price gap analysis were used to achieve the goals. In the Mandya district, almost 85% of farmers saw a reduction in their dairy farming income either during or after the lockdown. When compared to before the lockout, the net return per litre of milk for crossbreds with moderate output was down 52.42 percent in the Mandya district. During lockdown and post-lockdown periods in MANMUL, there was a decrease in the quantity of milk purchased and sold. While the amount of milk converted to SMP during lockdown increased due to a decline in milk sales. Curd and ghee sales among milk products declined both during and after the shutdown. In general, it is necessary to use current technology to raise the demand for milk and milk products. Therefore, in order to assure constant demand, milk unions should form partnerships with online consumer firms like Zomato, Swiggy, Dunzo, etc.

title: 121."I know prevention is better than cure sort of thing, but ...": barriers and facilitators to the implementation of on-farm preventive measures to reduce the risk of bovine tuberculosis on cattle farms in England.
abstract: Bovine Tuberculosis (bTB) is one of the most significant animal health challenges in the United Kingdom. Its associated control programme costs millions of pounds a year and has significant impacts on trade and human health via stakeholder burden. The Bovine Tuberculosis Advisory Service (TBAS) is a government-funded initiative run by private veterinarians in England to provide tailored advice to farmers on preventive measures to reduce the risk of bTB on their farms. However, there remains a need to improve understanding of the factors influencing the implementation of these measures, in order to identify ways in which the long-term success of the TBAS programme could be enhanced. The objectives of this study were to identify the barriers and facilitators that influence the implementation of preventive measures from the perspective of TBAS advisors and farmers who have participated in the initiative. A total of 13 semi-structured interviews were conducted with six farmers and seven TBAS advisors. Thematic analysis was undertaken using an inductive approach to identify barriers and facilitators to programme uptake. The identified sub-themes were then mapped deductively to the Capability, Opportunity, and Motivation Behaviour (COM-B) model (Michie et al. 2011). Factors relating to the overarching COM-B components of opportunity and motivation appeared to be key for decision-making. The barriers found primarily related to a lack of time, expense, and the perceived feasibility of implementing a recommended measure, the majority of which sat within the physical opportunity sub-component of the behavioural model. In addition, the importance of policy in terms of the social opportunity and reflective motivation sub-components was highlighted, and also acted as a barrier to the enaction of the recommendations. Facilitators and corresponding COM-B sub-components included ensuring a good farmer-advisor relationship (social opportunity), involving farmers in the decision-making process (reflective motivation) and a clear understanding of the rationale behind recommendations (psychological capability). By integrating this knowledge into the TBAS programme, including routes to overcoming barriers and utilising facilitators for farmers, advisors and policy makers, the implementation of bTB preventive measures is likely to be more successful and ultimately contribute to the goal of eradicating bTB.

title: 122.Machine Learning in commercial poultry farming: comparing standard and oriented bounding boxes in YOLOv11 for broiler detection.
abstract: -This study explores a practical application of Machine Learning (ML) for commercial poultry farming in the Philippines, addressing key challenges such as accurate stock density estimation and computational cost. While AI has demonstrated significant potential in livestock management, its adoption remains limited due to real-world farm constraints. By focusing on field conditions, this research aims to bridge the gap between advanced AI models and practical poultry farming needs. Specifically, this study evaluates how two AI models, YOLOv11 and YOLOv11-OBB, can be utilized in poultry farming. YOLO-based models have the potential to analyze broiler activities, assess poultry conditions, and explore additional ML applications in poultry monitoring. A key comparison is made between standard axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABB), which perform well in simple conditions, and oriented bounding boxes (OBB), which are better suited for high-density environments where birds may overlap or tilt. The goal is to determine which method offers greater accuracy, reliability, and adaptability in real-world farm operations. By prioritizing ease of use, real-time monitoring, and integration with farm management, this study aims to develop scalable, cost-effective AI solutions that enhance - not replace - farmworkers' efforts. The findings will contribute to the advancement of AI-powered poultry farming, improving broiler welfare, farm productivity, and decision-making in commercial operations.

title: 123.What does the large range in potential methane 'CO2 equivalent' evaluation imply for climate policy targets? An initial exploration in the context of agricultural emission scenarios for Northern Ireland.
abstract: As efforts to decrease greenhouse gas emissions and progress towards 'net-zero' intensify, increased scrutiny is being put on the role of the agricultural sector in climate change mitigation. Part of this has focussed on the balance of greenhouse gases associated with agriculture, with emissions dominated by methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O), in contrast to carbon dioxide (CO2) emissions, the main gas associated with fossil fuel combustion (and hence the energy and transport sectors). Conventionally, non-CO2gases are reported as 'CO2-equivalent' quantities, using the 100-year Global Warming Potential (GWP100) emission metric, and targets and other mitigation policy decisions typically utilise this metric. There are many other metric approaches, however, which can have very pronounced implications for the relative valuation of methane, in particular. Renewed focus on the challenges in comprehensive, cross-sectoral climate action has prompted discussion of whether metrics other than the GWP100 may have a role in policy formulation and especially target-setting. In Northern Ireland, these considerations are also reflected in climate legislation, where the Climate Change Act (Northern Ireland) 2022 notes the need to take account of "the distinct characteristics of biogenic methane." Here, I explore how near-term (2023-2027) agricultural emission reductions would be reported under multiple emission metrics (GWP100, GWP20, GTP100 and two applications of GWP*), to facilitate some of this consideration, and discuss potential implications for target-setting. The choice of metric has a marked impact on how highly agricultural methane emissions are valued (with respect to carbon dioxide), and GWP* in particular can reveal quite conceptually different information, with potentially significant implications if targets are set based on limiting sectoral contributions to overall temperature increase. Even if this framework is used, however, further emission reductions (or offsets) will be required in addition to those outlined in current plans. There are also still arguments for considering agricultural emissions in GWP100 terms, including that GWP100 'net-zero' is still ultimately required under national legislation. Recent United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) communications provide further discussion of how and why different metric approaches are so different, and highlight unresolved points in the role of metrics in climate policy.

title: 124.Breaking the barrier of human-annotated training data for machine-learning-aided plant research using aerial imagery.
abstract: Machine learning (ML) can accelerate biological research. However, the adoption of such tools to facilitate phenotyping based on sensor data has been limited by: (1) the need for a large amount of human-annotated training data for each context in which the tool is used; and (2) phenotypes varying across contexts defined in terms of genetics and environment. This is a major bottleneck because acquiring training data is generally costly and time-consuming. This study demonstrates how a ML approach can address these challenges by minimizing the amount of human supervision needed for tool building. A case study comparing ML approaches that examine images collected by an uncrewed aerial vehicle was performed to determine the presence of panicles (i.e., "heading") across thousands of field plots containing genetically diverse breeding populations of twoMiscanthusspecies. Automated analysis of aerial imagery enabled the identification of heading approximately nine times faster than in-field visual inspection by humans. Leveraging an Efficiently Supervised Generative and Adversarial Network (ESGAN) learning strategy reduced the requirement for human-annotated data by one to two orders of magnitude compared to traditional, fully supervised learning approaches. The ESGAN model learned the salient features of the dataset by using thousands of unlabeled images to inform the discriminative ability of a classifier so that it required minimal human-labeled training data. This method can accelerate the phenotyping of heading date as a measure of flowering time in Miscanthus across diverse contexts (e.g., in multi-state trials) and opens avenues to promote the broad adoption of ML tools.

title: 125.Effect of feed and season on physicochemical characteristics of milk and ripened Sicilo-Sarde ewe's cheese.
abstract: The fatty acid (FA) profile of milk and cheese is important for the consumer from a nutritional point of view. Feed is one of major effects influencing the milk and cheese properties. Thereby, the objective of this study was, to investigate the effect of feeding and season (in relation with feed) on Sicilo-Sarde ewes' milk and ripened pressed cheese. To do so, milk and cheese of three dairies (D1, D2 and D3) during three seasons (winter: S1, early spring: S2 and late spring: S3). were studied. Milk coagulation properties, physicochemical parameters, fatty acid composition of milk and cheese were carried out. Moreover, volatile profile of cheese was determined. D1 milk had higher (P < 0.001) fat (74%) and proteins (58%) comparing to D2 (64.8 and 51.7% for fat and protein respectively) and D3 (62.5% for fat and 56.6% for protein) diets. S3 milk was richer (P < 0.001) in fat (70.4 vs 66.3 and 64.7% respectively for S3, S2 and S1). Curd firmness was 28.5 mm for D2 vs 34.8 and 36.2 mm for D3 and D1, respectively. D1 cheese contained more fat (31.8%) and less protein (29.8%) comparing to D2 and D3 (30.3 and 31.33% for fat and protein, respectively) (P < 0.05). Contrarily to milk FA profile, cheese FA was mostly affected by season as S3 cheese was healthier and contained more polyunsaturated FA (4.91%; P < 0.01), desirable FA (40.9%; P < 0.001) and conjugated linoleic acid (0.9%; P < 0.001). It also tended to have lower saturated FA (67.7%), n6/n3 ratio (5.75) and lipid indices and higher monounsaturated FA (25.5%) comparing to S1 and S2. D2 cheese had slightly better health properties than D1 and D3. Acids were the major volatile compound (VC) in cheese. D2 cheese had higher levels of acids (P < 0.01) thus more VC (P < 0.001).

title: 126.Assessing autonomy and nutrient use efficiency of dairy sheep farming systems in Roquefort (France) through systemic nitrogen flow analysis.
abstract: CONTEXT: Because of climate change and the forecast trends, the sustainability and resilience of the intensified dairy sheep farming systems are threatened. To adapt, there is consensus about the interest in redesigning key farm operations (e.g. feeding system) by relying more on agroecological principles. OBJECTIVE: We aimed to characterize and assess a dairy sheep farming system in the main basin for this sector in France (Roquefort), to determine to what extent the quest for autonomy is at the expense of nutrient use efficiency, leading to identifying opportunities for improving sustainability METHODS: An in-depth analysis of nutrient flow was carried out by studying the nitrogen (N) flows with a systemic approach and using the ENA (ecological network analysis) methodology. Data were collected from the INRAE La Fage experimental farm, in Roquefort, France's main dairy sheep production region, during the period 2015-2019. Structural and agroecological indicators of the system's functioning were calculated. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: Farm feed (supplement) and forage autonomy were at 78.0 and 90.6%, respectively. On average, the system was up to 69% self-sufficient, indicating the existence of farming practices enhancing closing N cycles. The farming system's N efficiency was low (12.6%) compared to the N efficiency of the livestock (48.7%) and crops (65.0%) compartments considered separately; hence the importance of the holistic approach and the contribution of the various components of the livestock farming system for a better understanding of the system's performance-building process. The system's annual N flow network productivity was low (22.6 kg N ha-1). Overall, the system was strongly influenced by natural N inputs, especially rainfall and symbiotic fixation (49% of total inputs). Leaching caused most of the N losses within the system (67.0%) and represented 87.0% of the total arable land N losses. Overall, 80.0% of the effluents produced in the sheepfold were recycled through manure spreading in the cropping system plots to produce feed (i.e., hay, silage, and barley). Around half of the total system N flows were provided by internal nutrient flows between the crop and livestock sub-systems (45.0%) while 36.0% came from inputs. Results revealed high autonomy levels (78.0% for feed and 90.6% for forage), and opportunities to increase the overall farming system's performance mainly through reducing N losses and enhancing the nutrient use efficiency.

title: 127.Revised belowground factor reduces seed yield-based estimates of faba bean N2 fixation.
abstract: The incorporation of legumes, particularly faba bean (Vicia fabaL.), into cropping systems is pivotal for sustainable agriculture due to their ability to fix atmospheric nitrogen (N). Despite its significance, the quantification of biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) in faba bean remains challenging, particularly regarding the belowground (BG) contribution. This study updates the BG factor for BNF estimation using data from 42 primary studies reporting on both, measurements of above and belowground fixation. Total BNF based on dry matter seed yields was then recalculated with from a comprehensive dataset of 329 primary studies. A BG factor of 1.15 was derived, lower than widely used values, resulting in a total BNF estimate of 49 kg N per Mg dry matter seed yield. As a case study, the new estimation was applied for German national statistics data and compared with the legal framework for nutrient balances. This revealed an 18% overestimation of BNF and a twofold overestimation of nitrogen balances in official calculations, with implications for nutrient management policies. Our findings highlight the necessity of revising BNF estimates to improve the accuracy of rotational nitrogen budgeting and nutrient balance assessments. Faba beans remain a valuable crop for reducing synthetic N inputs, but precise quantification of their BNF potential is critical for informed decision-making and achieving sustainable agriculture.

title: 128.Contribution of new and old phosphorus from organic and inorganic fertilizers in subsurface-drained fields using machine learning.
abstract: Phosphorus is essential for crop growth, but it leaches through subsurface drainage discharge, impacting water quality. The objective was to (1) investigate the contributions of new and legacy phosphorus from organic and inorganic fertilizer sources in drainage discharge using machine learning, (2) assess the effect of manure timing on P loss. We collected data from two on-farm sites in southeast Michigan, USA. We applied the Weighted Regression on Discharge and Seasons (WRDS) equation to analyze P load based on drainage discharge and fertilizer application timing. The data was divided into calibration and validation, and a machine learning algorithm was employed to train the model, separately addressing event flow and base flow dynamics. Results showed KGE of 0.84 and NSE of 0.76, indicating a strong model prediction performance. The organic site had significantly higher new P losses, with new TP contributing 16.3% versus 2.9% and DRP 20.1% versus 0% (no measurable contribution) at the inorganic site. When applied during winter months, organic fertilizers contributed to extended periods of new P loss, whereas the early fall application resulted in lower new P loss, showing the importance of application timing. Legacy P was the primary source of TP losses(83.7%) and DRP (79.4%) at the organic site. Similarly, at the inorganic site, it accounted for 97.1% of TP and 100% of DRP losses. In conclusion, the machine learning algorithm provided a strong P loss prediction performance and showed that legacy P was the dominant source of P loss through drainage discharge.

title: 129.Data sovereignty and valuation model for sustainable agriculture innovation and equity.
abstract: This paper examines farmer data sovereignty and valuation approaches as critical elements for advancing sustainable agriculture. It analyses technological, educational, legal, economic, and methodological barriers to implementation, proposing a holistic approach to overcome these challenges. The study introduces an innovative data valuation model incorporating investment costs, potential commercial usage, and ecosystem services value, along with a framework for integrating this value into agricultural accounting practices. By exploring successful case studies, emerging technologies, and gender equity considerations, the paper offers insights for policymakers and stakeholders. It emphasizes the need for collaborative efforts between farmers, researchers, policymakers, and technology providers to create a more sustainable, resilient, and equitable agricultural system. The study concludes by outlining future research directions to further develop and refine these approaches in the context of evolving agricultural practices and technologies.

title: 130.Randomised controlled trial of a novel navel barrier solution versus strong iodine to protect navel and ear tag sites of neonatal lambs.
abstract: Background.During lambing 'strong' iodine (Iodine) is often used to protect neonatal navel and ear tag sites. Evidence for effectiveness is sparse. Recently, a navel barrier solution (NBS), with favourablein vitroproperties, was developed. Here anin vivotrial compared the two.

title: 131.Bibliometric analysis of sustainable agriculture research.
abstract: The volume of global research published on sustainable agriculture is growing fast, especially in China and India. Although the majority of research outputs came from high income countries in the past, middle-income countries have grown their share of global research steadily over the last 20 years and have been the majority shareholder since 2020. For research intensive countries, bilateral programmes that foster cooperation with researchers in the global south present a good opportunity to grow the existing research base. Sustainable agriculture publications represent around 0.1% to 0.3% of national output for major research economies. For African countries, the percentage is much higher (0.8% for Nigeria and 1.5% for Ghana), indicating a proportionally higher level of investment in this area compared to all other research topics. Most authors publish more research that explicitly mentions locations in their home countries than in foreign countries, with Nigeria, Ghana, and Brazil all ranking in the top 10 in terms of relative volume. Some research-intensive countries, such as the United Kingdom, published research that refers to countries across many continents, typically through collaboration with local partners. Over the survey period, the percentage of internationally collaborative publications has grown steadily for the United Kingdom, from approximately 50% in 2008 to over 75% in 2023, in line with other high-income countries. Nigeria is also collaborating more, increasing its share to around 60% since 2022, similar to Ghana, which itself has one of the highest collaboration rates with low-income countries. Brazil collaborates less frequently than the other three countries, around 45% in recent years with no significant upward trend. Most international collaboration occurs within three main clusters, one containing European institutions, one containing Canadian and United States institutions, and the other Chinese. CGIAR research institutes play an important role in developing collaboration across these clusters and within specific countries in Africa and Asia. Topics of research in sustainable agriculture are diverse, covering various crop and crop management schemes, plant biology, geosciences, data and remote sensing, modelling, and in a range of policy areas, such as sustainable development, climate change adaptation, and conservation agriculture. Benchmarking countries using bibliometric indicators across a range of topics provides useful insights regarding their capacity, growth, and prior collaborations that could be used to inform future investments. A range of award mechanisms, such as studentships, mobility grants, fellowships, project grants, and partnership building schemes, could be targeted according to individual country-topic profiles. Although the United Kingdom has already established links with Nigeria and Ghana through publication collaboration (104 and 82 papers, respectively, since 2000), ties are spread thinly over partnerships between many different research institutions. Only two pairs (University of Birmingham University of Nigeria and University of Leeds Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology in Ghana) have co-authored five or more publications since 2000. Brazil has yet to establish significant links with Nigeria or Ghana. 15 percent of sustainable agriculture research has been cited in policy documents, usually within five years of publication, with some topics (e.g. Sustainable Food System and Food Waste) receiving attention from policy sources in shorter timeframes. Research that mentions locations in low-income countries receives more policy citations on average than countries in other income groups.

title: 132.Adaptive Corn Management Systems (ACMS) for optimizing agronomic performance in the Mid-Atlantic U.S.
abstract: Corn (Zea maysL.) yield is influenced by complex factors including erratic weather, disease, stress, and inconsistent nutrient use efficiency that challenge optimal yield. Standard management recommendations often fall short, prompting interest in intensive strategies within an Adaptive Corn Management System (ACMS). To investigate this, we employed an addition/omission technique within a randomized complete block design (RCBD) to compare Cooperative Extension standard corn management recommendations with an intensive protocol aimed at identifying yield-limiting factors. Our intensive approach (check) combined early-season biostimulant applications with mid-season supplementation of phosphorus (P), potassium (K), and nitrogen (N) at the V7 stage, followed by foliar fungicides and additional foliar N at the R1 stage. Field trials spanned five Virginia locations over 2022 and 2023 under both irrigated and non-irrigated conditions, yielding 10 site-years of data. Analysis via ANOVA in JMP® Version 18 with Dunnett's test revealed that the intensive approach increased grain yield in 3 of 10 experiments. Under non-irrigated conditions, the intensive check averaged a 5.9% yield increase over the standard check. In irrigated trials, standard check yielded 34% compared to 8.9% in intensive check over non-irrigated with site-specific irrigation impacts ranging from 14% to 61%, emphasizing site-specific intensification strategies for yield enhancement.

title: 133.Farmingpy: Python package for developing digital twins and precision farming data processing.
abstract: Digital twins of cropping systems are under development aiming towards better forecasting and decision-making on farms. A Python package called farmingpy was developed to support the development of digital twins combining machinery data and remote sensing data with the APSIM simulation model. The package can also be used for other precision farming data processing tasks. Shared open-source software packages can provide generic modules and assist the digital twin development processes by reducing duplication of work. The aim of this paper is to present the farmingpy Python package including two use case examples.

title: 134.Sustainable control of parasites in ewes (SCOPE): pre-registration of protocol for a randomised controlled trial on the use of moxidectin in ewes at lambing time.
abstract: Background: Helminth infections are a major economic and welfare burden to UK ruminant production enterprises, costing the UK sheep industry an estimated £41m annually. Anthelmintic resistance (AR) in sheep gastrointestinal nematodes (GIN) is ubiquitous and increasing on European sheep farms, threatening farmers' ability to adequately control these parasites in the longer term. GIN infections in periparturient ewes are of particular concern as GIN eggs excreted by ewes are a primary source of infection for lambs. Most UK farmers use anthelmintics to treat ewes at lambing time, potentially selecting for AR. This selection may be offset by reduced lamb worm burden and, thus, the number of anthelmintic treatments that lambs require. We urgently need to develop evidence-based guidelines for sustainable nematode control in periparturient ewes. However, evidence of the impact of treating periparturient ewes on the development of AR is conflicted. To date, no controlled, randomised study investigating the impact of ewe treatments on productivity and AR has been conducted in the UK/Europe, and no studies of this nature have investigated the use of moxidectin.
