Objectives: This trial will investigate the impacts of long-acting moxidectin versus short-acting moxidectin or targeted selective treatment of peri-parturient ewes on measures of health and productivity of ewes and their offspring, and on GIN population genetic structure over time. Study design: Randomised Controlled Trial. Methods: Sixty healthy Lleyn-X ewes and their twin lambs (120 lambs) will be randomly assigned, by stratified block randomisation, to three treatment groups (long-acting moxidectin, short-acting moxidectin and targeted selective treatment) in the University of Liverpool's commercial lowland flock at Ness Heath Farm (Cheshire, UK). Ewes and their lambs will graze separately by treatment group. Performance and parasitological parameters will be measured between lambing and finishing (reaching target weight), and GIN eggs and larvae collected from faeces and pasture will be subjected to ITS-2 rDNA nemabiome metabarcoding and mtDNA marker sequencing to quantify changes in GIN population genetic structure over time. The trial will be repeated, with a different sample of randomly assigned ewes each year, for two consecutive years (2025 and 2026) to account for weather-dependent interannual variability and to monitor impacts over two consecutive grazing seasons. Data will be analysed according to intention-to-treat principles. Reporting findings: Findings will be communicated to industry stakeholders in a report co-produced with project partner SCOPS (Sustainable Control of Parasites in Sheep) and published in a peer-reviewed journal.

title: 135.Analyzing the inoculation effects of three of Trichoderma spp. species on two Brachiaria spp. species.
abstract: Trichodermaare fungi that associate with plants' roots and other cortical layers, solubilizing substrate nutrients, making them available for absorption, and controlling pathogens that attack these structures. The genusBrachiariais currently well-established in Brazil, occupying around 99 million hectares of land, being of great contribution to the national forage farming. Despite the numerous advantages presented by the genusTrichodermaand the genusBrachiaria, no previous reports in the literature analyze the effects of inoculatingBrachiariaroots withTrichodermaspores. Following this rationale, this study aims to analyze the effects of inoculation using threeTrichodermaspecies on twoBrachiariaspecies. In a greenhouse, theBrachiaria decumbensandBrachiaria brizanthawere sown in pots and inoculated withT. asperellum,T. atroviride,T. harzianum, and combinations between them at 107spores/ml. Dry mass and chlorophyll values were measured 12 and 24 weeks after sowing, and moisture, leaf area, and number of tillers at 12 weeks after sowing. There was no significant difference considering treatment forB. brizantha. However, the combination betweenT. asperellum&T. harzianumincreased the number of tillers forB. decumbens. This represented the first attempt to inoculate the roots ofBrachiariaspecies withTrichodermaspecies alone or combined, paving the road for future studies.

title: 136.Machine and deep learning-based wheat yield prediction: the critical role of soil moisture and remote sensing data.
abstract: Food security is an increasingly pressing challenge that can be tackled through advanced technologies designed to monitor agroecosystems and facilitate timely, data-driven decisions. Integrating innovative technologies is crucial for enhancing agricultural sustainability and resilience, thereby contributing to global food security. This study compares traditional machine learning algorithms - support vector machine (SVM) and random forest (RF) with a deep learning algorithm, deep neural network (DNN), for wheat yield prediction using satellite-derived data. Two feature sets were utilized: (M1) vegetation indices combined with weather variables (traditional method) and (M2) M1, along with surface soil moisture (SSM) (our innovative approach). Results indicate that the optimal prediction window spans from the onset of stem elongation to the initiation of flowering (BBCH 30-61), during which the average R2, RMSE, and MAE were 0.76, 484.04 kg ha-1, and 281.90 kg ha-1, respectively. At this stage, the DNN achieved the highest performance with M1 (R2= 0.73, RMSE = 502.59 kg ha-1, MAE = 338.51 kg ha-1) and improved further with M2 (R2= 0.85, RMSE = 379.93 kg ha-1, MAE = 244.22 kg ha-1). Additionally, when paired with M2, SVM and RF outperformed the DNN trained on M1. The feature-importance analysis revealed that Near-Infrared Reflectance of Vegetation (NIRv) was the most significant predictor, slightly surpassing the Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) and SSM. These findings underscore the critical role of surface soil moisture in enhancing model accuracy across growth stages and emphasize the importance of selecting a well-balanced feature set rather than relying solely on complex models. A carefully curated set of features boosts model performance, ensuring more reliable yield predictions for various agricultural applications.

title: 138.Transmission of highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1 to calves fed unpasteurized milk from experimentally infected cows.
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b genotype B3.13 was confirmed in a dairy cow in Texas on March 25, 2024, by the US Department of Agriculture (USDA) National Veterinary Services Laboratories (NVSL) in response to a multi-state investigation into milk production losses. The amount and duration of virus shed in milk from the inoculated mammary quarters point to milk as a primary source of virus spread within and between dairy herds. Pasteurization has been shown to inactive the virus in milk, however, domestic cats consuming raw milk from affected cows developed fatal systemic influenza infection. Investigations on affected dairy herds demonstrated the presence of viral RNA in milk samples for up to 2 weeks before the appearance of clinical signs and diagnostic confirmation of infection. During this lag, unpasteurized milk may pose a risk to calves. Here, we sought to determine if H5N1 genotype B3.13 strain could be transmitted to calves fed unpasteurized milk from virus positive lactating cows. Five Holstein calves of approximately 7 to 11 weeks old were fed 0.95 L of unpasteurized milk twice a day via bucket. Milk was collected from two lactating Holstein cows inoculated by an intramammary route and fed to four calves for four days. Milk from two non-inoculated cows was fed to one negative control calf for four days. After four days all five calves were fed milk from non-inoculated cows. Calves fed infected milk showed clinical signs including nasal discharge, mild fever, mild lethargy, loose stool and slightly increased respiratory effort for 5-6 days. Signs of clinical disease were mild and may not be recognized under field conditions with other environmental or health stressors. Viral RNA was consistently detected in nasal swabs from all four calves from 2 to 4 DPI, with consistent detection persisting after calves were transitioned to being fed milk from non-inoculated cows. Infection was confirmed by viral RNA detected in nasal swabs, antigen and viral RNA detection in lung lesions, lymph nodes and pharyngeal tonsil, and seroconversion. Ct values of the nasal swabs were significantly correlated (-0.55) with lethargy in the calves. As Ct values dropped, and viral load increased, calves became more lethargic. Milk diverted from the human food supply in H5N1 positive dairy herds or from suspect cows should not be fed to calves without pasteurization. The determination of routes of transmission like the study described here is an essential first step to inform subsequent research on intervention and vaccination strategies.

title: 139.Direct and indirect cocoa deforestation in the tropical moist forests of Ghana.
abstract: Across the tropics, cocoa is one of the main drivers of deforestation. In Ghana, the world's second largest cocoa producer, the role of each of the main economic sectors in driving deforestation remains, however, contested - with cocoa, mining, logging, and plantations each blaming the others. Previous work has also suggested that food crops are displaced into forests by cocoa expansion, raising concerns about indirect land use change and impacts on food availability. Here, using satellite-based maps and secondary statistics, we quantify the direct deforestation drivers between 2000 and 2019 in the entire cocoa-growing region of Ghana. Then, we use a land-balance approach to assess the indirect role of the expansion of land uses in food crop deforestation. We find that cocoa is the major direct driver (~57%), followed by food crops and logging (~39% in total). Roughly 30% of the deforestation and degradation linked to food crops could be attributed to their displacement by other land uses - with 15% (9%-17%) due to cocoa expansion into food crops. In cocoa-saturated regions, indirect cocoa deforestation is likely to increase as forests only remain in gazetted areas, where growing food crops is either legal or more tolerated by officials than cocoa. Accounting for its direct and indirect role, cocoa is associated with ~20% of the deforestation in gazetted areas. This research highlights the need to move away from sustainability efforts targeting one single commodity at a time to more transformative approaches that develop a coordinated vision across the food and land system. Such a vision would regulate multiple commodities holistically, address lock-ins, and reconsider the overall goals of land systems in the region (how much land should be dedicated to cocoa, how and for whose benefits).
authors: Erasmus K. H. J. zu Ermgassen

title: 140.Estimating leaf nitrogen concentration of grain sorghum, corn, and forage sorghum with hyperspectral data and vegetation indices from a spectroradiometer.
abstract: Nitrogen deficiency in plants is often done by visual scoring. Spectroradiometers have been identified as a promising alternative to visual scoring because they can give information about plants' stress in the shortest time. Therefore, this study was carried out to identify the regions of the electromagnetic spectrum (EMS) that are related to leaf N and to determine how well we can use vegetation indices to estimate leaf nitrogen concentration (LNC). Conducted in a controlled greenhouse in Stillwater, Oklahoma, from August to October 2021, the experiment involved three crops grain sorghum, corn, and forage sorghum and four nitrogen levels (20%, 50%, 75%, and 100% of Hoagland's nutrient solution). The crops were grown in a split-plot design with controlled drip irrigation. Some crop physiological data, LNC, and reflectance data were taken. The results showed the possibility of using hyperspectral data to predict LNC with vegetation indices effectively estimating LNC. Among the indices tested, the Transformed Chlorophyll Absorption in Reflectance Index (TCARI) performed best, with an R2 of 0.72 in relation to LNC. Multiple linear regression (MLR) using the best vegetation indices (VIs) improved the estimation accuracy further, achieving an R2 of 0.77. These findings demonstrate that leaf spectral reflectance and vegetation indices can provide a fast, cost-effective way to monitor nitrogen status in bioenergy crops during the growing season. The study highlights the potential of hyperspectral reflectance to aid in precision agriculture by enabling rapid, in-season adjustments to nitrogen application, thereby improving crop management and productivity.

title: 141.Exploring methodological challenges in wetland valuation: a comprehensive review of global wetland valuation methods and applications.
abstract: The valuation of wetlands is integral to their conservation and sustainable management, yet methodological challenges persist in accurately assessing their worth. Drawing from diverse sources including the Ramsar Convention on Wetlands repository, EconPapers, Wetlands International publications, and databases such as Environmental Valuation Reference Inventory, this review critically evaluates existing wetland valuation methodologies and identifies key gaps in research. Market-based, non-market, and cost-based approaches are analyzed, highlighting their theoretical foundations, strengths, and limitations. Through a synthesis of literature, recurring themes and knowledge gaps are elucidated, providing insights into the current landscape of wetland valuation. Strategies for addressing methodological gaps are proposed, emphasizing the need for modifications to existing methods, integration of diverse valuation techniques, and further research and development. Examining global applications of these methods reveals challenges and opportunities influenced by socio-economic and cultural factors. Based on the review, recommendations are provided to enhance methodological rigor and practical application in decision-making processes. This comprehensive assessment underscores the importance of addressing methodological gaps for effective wetland conservation and sustainable development. Through collaboration and continued research efforts, the full value of wetlands can be accurately recognized and preserved for future generations.

title: 142.A comparative analysis of biochar's role in enhancing late-season growth and yield of cruciferous vegetables in coastal Bangladesh.
abstract: Coastal Bangladesh faces significant agricultural challenges due to saline soils, nutrient deficiencies, and environmental stressors, particularly during the late growing season. This study evaluates the comparative effects of biochar application on the growth and yield of cauliflower (Brassica oleraceavar.botrytis) and broccoli (Brassica oleraceavar. italica) under these conditions. Biochar, a carbon-rich soil amendment, has been shown to improve soil fertility, water retention, and salinity mitigation, making it a promising solution for sustainable crop production. Using a two-way ANOVA, the study examined the impact of biochar at four application rates (2, 4, 6, and 8 tons/ha) on key growth parameters, including plant height, leaf size, curd weight, and yield. Results revealed that while biochar significantly improved growth metrics across both crops, cauliflower demonstrated a more pronounced response in terms of yield and curd weight. Early-stage growth (15 days) showed transient improvements in leaf number, while leaf size and curd weight benefits persisted throughout the season. Interaction effects between crop type and biochar treatment were crop-specific, highlighting the need for tailored application strategies. This research underscores biochar's potential to enhance late-season growth and yield in coastal regions, offering critical insights for optimizing agricultural practices in resource-constrained environments.

title: 143.Genomic analysis of dry date palm fruit size traits and identification of candidate genes through GWAS.
abstract: The commercial value of economically significant fruits, including date palm fruit (dates), is influenced by various factors, such as biochemical composition and morphological features like size, shape, and visual appearance, which are key determinants of their quality and market value. Dates are typically consumed at the dry stage (Tamar), during which they exhibit a wide range of physical characteristics, such as color, length, weight, and skin appearance. Understanding the genetic basis of these traits is crucial for improving crop quality and breeding new cultivars. In this study, we integrated a genome dataset from highly diverse date cultivars with phenotypes of dry fruit such as length, width, area, and weight, identifying multiple significant genetic loci (SNPs) associated with these traits. We also identified candidate genes located near the associated SNPs that are involved in biological processes such as cell differentiation, proliferation, growth, and the regulation of signalling pathways for growth regulators like auxin and abscisic acid, as observed in other plants. Gene expression analysis reveals that many of these genes are highly expressed in the early stage of fruit development when the fruit attains its maximum size and weight. These findings will enhance our understanding of genetic determinants of fruit size particularly at the commercially important Tamar stage.

title: 144.Optimizing a protocol for salinity recovery during seedling stage in rice.
abstract: Salinity is one of the major abiotic stresses affecting rice production, but the levels of salinity in a given field are not constant across the growing season. Since the level of salinity stress a plant experiences can fluctuate, fast recovery from salinity stress may be a useful trait to improve rice productivity in salinity-prone areas. To develop a protocol to screen for salinity recovery, seedling stage hydroponic experiments were conducted to measure salinity recovery over time through both destructive and high-throughput image-based phenotyping. Seven rice varieties were included that had previously been classified as tolerant or susceptible to salinity. Following exposure to seedling stage salinity, plants were transferred to solution with no added salt and allowed to recover. Green leaf area and relative growth rates (RGR) of salinity tolerant varieties and one salinity sensitive variety initiated recovery (i.e. started to increase) after four days of salt stress removal and required six days to completely recover (i.e., to resume a similar RGR to that observed in the no-salt control treatment), while the other salinity sensitive varieties took more time to recover. Therefore, an optimal recovery period of six days after salt stress removal was identified for screening. Some salinity sensitive varieties were able to recover based on RGR and chlorophyll fluorescence values, while their Na+contents remained high. Therefore, salinity tolerance may not necessarily correspond to salinity recovery ability. The protocol optimized here can be scaled up to screen diversity panels and populations and used for genetic mapping of the seedling stage salinity recovery trait.

title: 146.Accuracy in agricultural citizen science: farmers' assessment of harvest output in Ghana.
abstract: This study investigates methods for farmer-led yield estimation in decentralized on-farm trials in Ghana. Decentralized trials are key to reaching remote communities and reducing costs, but often require physical presence during time-sensitive tasks. Farmer participation in data collection, especially if data can be shared digitally, may help overcome these constraints. Farmers' accuracy in measuring harvest output is often unknown, and therefore leads to falling back on technicians. This study determines the accuracy of farmer measurement outputs and determinants of the accuracy by using simple on-farm exercises in which farmers execute the estimation and measurement tasks. We tested yield estimation methods, including volumetric measurement and weighing of maize kernels and cocoa beans, to evaluate farmers' accuracy. Volumetric measurement, involving a container of known volume, proved robust and accurate without prior training, performing consistently across farmers with various education levels. Weighing with scales, while theoretically more precise, was error-prone, even after training, due to issues with scales and taring. Refinements such as using electronic scales and obviating tare adjustments could improve weighing accuracy. Volumetric measurement emerged as a practical solution, especially where training is limited, offering consistent results. The results of this study provide important information to researchers on the type and the magnitude of error that they can expect when farmers measure harvest output. Our findings suggest that decentralized trials relying on farmer measurements can expand trial reach, reduce geographical bias, and optimize resource use by decreasing reliance on technician visits.

title: 147.Combining mobile proximal soil sensors and a crop model to produce high spatial resolution yield prediction maps.
abstract: Precision agriculture requires a detailed knowledge of the within-field variation of yield forming factors and the productivity potential of each field area. Proximal soil sensing can effectively produce soil properties maps (e.g. soil texture), which combined with crop growth models, can be used to estimate the crop's needs at high resolution within the field. The goal of this work was to use a case study to test all the steps of the process of creating a yield map from mobile soil sensors and determine the impact of uncertainties and inaccuracies on the results. Soil texture maps (0- 90 cm of depth) of a field were derived from mobile sensors and used as input for the process based deterministic crop growth model HERMES to produce a high-resolution yield map. Compared to actual yield maps, the simulated yield map successfully identified the major differences in productivity within the field, although some spatial variation was lost during the simulation, mostly at the point of translating soil texture maps into soil water retention parameters. The model also showed a tendency of overestimating yield across the entire field. A crop model simulation based on measured soil parameters resulted in a yield prediction accuracy of about 10% higher than a simulation based on estimated (mapped) soil parameters. In conclusion: (a) the loss of heterogeneity, although measurable, occurred at a scale that might not have a significant impact on the site-specific management plan.; (b) most yield map inaccuracies can be attributed more to model calibration than to the mapping process itself.

title: 148.Growth, yield, and economic viability of Withania somnifera in agroforestry systems: a comparison of tree species in Charland, Bangladesh.
abstract: Ashwagandha (Withania somnifera) offers economic and therapeutic benefits in Bangladesh, enhancing farmers' profits and addressing the rising demand for natural health products. Its integration into woodlots and orchards can increase both income and productivity. However, research on its yield and economic viability in agroforestry systems with different tree species is limited, underscoring the need for further study. To reduce this knowledge gap, an experiment was conducted from June to December, 2022 in Char Kalibari, Sadar upazila, Mymensingh district of Bangladesh, aimed to evaluate the growth and yield ofWithania somniferaunder three tree species -Swietenia macrophylla(mahogany),Mangifera indica(mango), andCitrus sinensis(malta) - and to assess the economic viability ofWithania somnifera-based agroforestry systems in Charland (bars). A single-factor randomized complete block design with four treatments and three replications was employed, resulting in a total of 12 plots, each measuring 16 m2. The treatments consisted of T0, representingWithania somniferasole cropping (control), T1 asWithania somnifera-Swietenia macrophyllaagroforestry (WSAF), T2 asWithania somnifera-Mangifera indicaagroforestry (WMAF), and T3 asWithania somnifera-Citrus sinensisagroforestry (WCAF).Withania somniferaseedlings were transplanted into the interspaces, where the trees were permanently planted at a spacing of 2 meters (m) × 2 m. The results revealed thatWithania somniferain sole cropping had the best growth and highest dry root yield (692.0933 kg/ha), with significant differences in height, root length, and diameter compared to agroforestry treatments. Among the agroforestry combinations, the WSAF performed better than others, while the WCAF system showed the lowest growth and yield due to increased competition. Economically, the WMAF system provided the highest net income (3267.78 US$/ha) and benefit-cost ratio (3.38), making it the most profitable agroforestry combination. Correlation analyses indicated strong positive relationships between yield and key yield-contributing traits, such as root number, length, and diameter. In summary, the limited negative impact of tree components onWithania somniferaemphasizes the viability of its cultivation in agroforestry systems in the Charland area to meet national demand.

title: 149.Evaluating clinical mastitis in four dimensions: Part I. Defining the production, immunological, clinical and pathogen severity.
abstract: Assessing the severity of clinical mastitis (CM) is a critical step in making treatment decisions 26 and plays a crucial role in mastitis control and ensuring animal welfare. The prevailing method 27 for assessing the severity of CM mainly considers clinical symptoms. However, the severity of 28 CM can be assessed from various perspectives. This study aims to define and assess CM 29 severity in four dimensions: production, immunology, clinic, and pathogen. We collected data 30 on naturally occurring CM cases on three robotic dairy farms in Belgium (N = 2) and the 31 Netherlands (N = 1), involving four types of information: quarter-level milk yield, cow-level 32 somatic cell count (SCC), clinical symptoms, and causative pathogens. The final dataset for 33 analysis included 129 CM cases detected by the herdsmen from 105 cows and 113 lactations. 34 In the production dimension, CM severity was defined based on the maximum relative quarter35 level milk loss for the clinically inflamed and clinically uninflamed quarters separately. In the 36 immunological dimension, severity was defined based on the deviation of the cow-level SCC 37 from a cow-level baseline. The clinical dimension used existing scoring and stratified between 38 mild, moderate and severe cases. Finally, the severity in the pathogen dimension was based on 39 the bacteriological culture results of a milk sample collected from the inflamed quarter on the 40 detection day. For each dimension, scores between farms, parities, and lactation stages (LS) 41 were compared. A significant difference was only found between farms, both in the production 42 and clinical dimension. Combining the four scores may help to capture the full scope of CM 43 by simultaneously assessing the severity of cases across production, immunological, clinical, 44 and pathogen-related dimensions.

title: 150.Evaluating clinical mastitis in four dimensions: Part II. Correlation analysis between production, immunological, clinical and pathogen severity.
abstract: The severity of clinical mastitis (CM) can be assessed in four dimensions: production, immunological, clinical, and pathogen. Each dimension contains different information about the CM case. Both the level of severity in each dimension and their within-case correlation could help to get a thorough image of the disease. This information can be crucial to further substantiate and refine treatment decisions and understand the recovery process. This study aimed to investigate the correlations between these four dimensions of CM severity in a group of 129 naturally occurring CM cases at 3 farms in Belgium (N = 2) and the Netherlands (N = 1). To this end, we first performed an exploratory analysis by grouping CM cases based on their CM severity in one dimension and comparing the distributions of CM severity in the other dimensions. Next, the Spearman correlation matrix of CM severity between the four dimensions was calculated. Finally, to investigate the relations between severity dimensions among farms, parities and lactation stages (LS), we implemented linear fixed effect models. The severity dimensions exhibited positive correlations with each other, with Spearman correlation coefficients ranging from 0.3 to 0.5. The fixed effects models revealed that parity and LS have significant impacts on the relations between certain dimensions. For example, early LS exhibited different linear relationships between the immunological and production dimensions, suggesting that hormonal changes and energy distribution during this period may influence their associations. These results demonstrate that, although the CM severity scores in the four dimensions are positively correlated with each other, some variations exist between them.

title: 151.How do neglected and underutilised crops (NUCS) in Africa contribute to food security, nutrition and climate change outcomes: a scoping review protocol.
abstract: Building a more resilient food system requires growing crops that are adapted to variable environments- more heat, less moisture, greater pressure from pests and diseases, frequent extreme weather conditions like droughts and floods, inherently weak structured soils. Historically, plant breeding investments have been highly concentrated in cash crops and major staple crops like maise, wheat, and rice. Plant breeding investment in Africa has largely focused on the most economically important crops, like maise, tobacco, cotton, coffee, and cocoa, although some attention has been paid to legumes (including, cowpea and bambara groundnuts). Crops such as millets (i.e., sorghum, fonio, finger and pearl millets), which are utilised and most adapted to smallholder farmer's conditions, have not received as much investment as staple crops. According to the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA) is one of the global regions with the least adaptive capacity to climate change. Current climate change predictions for the region paint a scenario of rising temperatures, increased variability in rainfall (change in patterns, onset and amounts) and increased frequency of extreme weather events such as drought, heat, combined drought and heat and floods. It is already experiencing some of these weather extremes with drought and floods ravaging most of SSA's landscape. Agricultural production is of particular concern. Small-scale producers in low- and middle-income countries are among those whose livelihoods are most vulnerable to climate change (Davis et al., 2022). The number of poor people dependent on agriculture and food systems in low- and lower-middle income countries is large-nearly 3.2 billion people live in rural areas, and most still depend to varying degrees on agriculture and food systems for their livelihoods (Lipper et al., 2020). Most of SSA's economies are still heavily dependent (directly or indirectly) on agriculture as a driver of economic and rural development. This is of great concern when viewed within the context of the impacts climate change will have on agriculture, and the vulnerability of rural households and the urban poor, regarding food and nutrition security, because the incidence of crop failure will likely increase. A healthy diet - one that prevents multi-nutrient deficiencies and excesses related to a variety of diseases - depends on consumption of a wide diversity of foods, including whole grains, legumes, nuts, fruits, vegetables, animal products, roots, and tubers. Notably, one of the key indicators of food security is the availability and accessibility of diversified food sources by individuals to meet their nutritional dietary requirements and enhance their healthy wellbeing (FAO; Chivenge et al, 2015). More recently, breeding of highly nutritious traditional, indigenous, and orphan crops has received increased attention. Some of the most micronutrient and protein-rich crops, like legumes, seeds, fruits, and vegetables, receive little-to-no breeding research and investment, but a diet incorporating a variety of NUCS offers improved nutrition and overall health, while also providing extra advantages for human productivity and livelihoods. This has led to heavy dependency on a few crops, lack of resilience in food systems, and an increase in dependency on commodity crops, as well as malnutrition and undernutrition.

title: 152.Advanced segmentation of soil constituents in X-ray CT images using nnUNet.
abstract: Segmentation of soil constituents in X-ray CT imagery is critical for advancing our understanding of soil structure dynamics, but challenges arise due to the overlapping X-ray attenuation. In this study, we explore the potential of nnUNet, a deep learning-based semantic segmentation model, for applications in soil science. We evaluated nnUNet on three challenging datasets: (1) heterogeneous soil structure with numerous material classes sharing gray value ranges, (2) fine roots in noisy images, and (3) permafrost core with gradual gray value transitions between sediment types. The performance of nnUNet was compared to other reference methods, namely ilastik, Rootine v.2 and manual thresholding. For Dataset 1, the segmentation accuracy surpassed that of ilastik for the particulate organic matter class. Dataset-specific challenges, such as annotating fine structures (Dataset 2) or poorly defined boundaries between material classes (Dataset 3), impacted the performance of nnUNet, compared to more specialized methods. The mean validation Dice scores were 0.71, 0.90, 0.92, for Dataset 1, 2 and 3, respectively, which suggested overall good model performance. Our study underscores that deep learning models like nnUNet perform well for the segmentation of complex soil structures and could assist the development of a generalized segmentation model, thereby fostering standardization in soil structure analysis.

title: 153.Addressing usability challenges to enhance data quality and efficiency in crowdsourced food system data.
abstract: Generating digitalized, mobile-phone-based data can transform food systems research. Challenges, including network accessibility, infrastructure, and reliance on users' basic digital literacy, and user familiarity with data-collection modalities, create usability issues that constrain user participation and data quality. Evidence of systematic usability research on mobile phone data-collection tools in development contexts is limited. Our study presents a mixed-methods approach for testing the usability of an unstructured supplementary service-data system, deployed on mobile phones in Rwanda. Combining heuristic evaluation and usability testing among eight respondents, we identified system-design and usability faults, and suggested fixes for system redesign. Issues identified included difficulties with starting and completing the survey; challenges in comprehending the question-and-answer format; and the constraints of users' low digital literacy. Comparing our results with those from previous data collection, we observed that the fixes statistically improved a dietary-recall survey response rate from 58% to 70% and reduced the number of low-quality responses from 24% to 11%, with the greatest improvements observed among female respondents. These results demonstrate how, with a moderate, up-front cost, integrating a relatively simple testing set-up into a design process can generate significant performance and output quality improvements. As mobile phones will remain the principal technology for data collection in lower and low- middle income countries, it is imperative that digital data collection system design is as intuitive, inclusive, and user-friendly as possible. Deploying human-centered design approaches can ensure this, and support generating high-quality, representative, and cost-effective data.

title: 154.Enhancing phytochemical composition and nutritional profiles in common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) varieties through roasting.
abstract: Common beans (Phaseolus vulgarisL.) are rich in protein and their combination of carbohydrates, dietary fiber, and minerals makes them a unique healthy food. This study examines the effects of oven roasting at 110°C for 70 minutes on the phytochemical content, antinutrient levels, phytosterols, and lipid profiles of 12 varieties of common bean (Phaseolus vulgarisL.) flours. Results revealed significant changes in phytochemical composition and antinutritional factors post-roasting, with notable variations among bean varieties. Stigmasterol and ß-sitosterol were the predominant phytosterols, influencing the lipid profile of both raw and roasted beans. Roasting conditions, including temperature and time, have a significant role to play in the stability and concentration of these compounds, suggesting the influence of heat-induced chemical reactions. Correlation analysis highlighted strong associations between phytochemicals, antioxidants, and nutritional components. The principal component analysis identified distinct clusters among bean varieties based on their phytochemical and antioxidant profiles, with pigmented varieties exhibiting enhanced nutritional content. These findings underscore the importance of understanding roasting's impact on common bean composition, informing strategies for maximizing their nutritional value in both dietary and industrial applications.

title: 155.Pedotransfer functions and their impact on soil water dynamics simulation and yield prediction.
abstract: Pedotransfer functions used to determine water retention parameters from more readily available soil 47 attributes (texture, soil organic carbon) may have a big impact on soil water dynamics and yield 48 simulations by crop models. In this study we used the model HERMES to quantify and understand the 49 impact of seven pedotransfer functions and two pedotransfer function ensemble models on crop yield 50 on sites with variable texture using water retention parameters (i.e. field capacity, wilting point and total 51 pore space) derived from the pedotransfer functions. Additionally, a continuous synthetic soil database 52 was created to assess the effect of gradual changes in soil texture on yield simulation. The accuracy of 53 the soil water dynamics simulations with the different pedotransfer functions was determined using soil 54 water measurements at the test sites. The impact of pedotransfer functions on yield simulations was 55 assessed by quantifying the yield differences at the experimental sites and across the synthetic soil 56 database. The choice of pedotransfer functions resulted in most cases in measurable differences in soil 57 water content dynamics, often showing a direct relationship between field capacity and water content. 58 Often, pedotransfer functions producing higher estimated field capacity also resulted in higher yield, 59 indicating that model yield simulation is sensitive to soil water availability. Pedotransfer functions 60 showed an increasing variability in water retention parameters estimation and yield simulation at 61 specific points in the sand percent continuum of the synthetic soil database, indicating that these 62 functions can be sensitive even to small changes in particle size distribution.

title: 156.The status of academic research on salmon farming: a scoping review protocol.
abstract: Salmon aquaculture (variously Atlantic and Pacific) has rapidly expanded across Norway, Chile, Canada, and Scotland, amongst others, driven by advancements in technology and market dynamics. However, this growth has spurred debates around environmental and socio-economic sustainability, especially concerning environmental degradation and "food imperialism." The intensive industry, once purported to be essential for global protein supply, is now scrutinised for prioritising luxury markets over food security and for its high ecological and social impacts, including pollution, disease spread, feed supply chain effects, and damaging livelihoods and standards of living. Climate change intensifies these concerns, with rising sea temperatures and extreme weather exacerbating disease and infrastructure risks, for example. Furthermore, the industry's reaction to activism raises issues of transparency and public accountability. With high mortality rates and substantial welfare concerns, the sector faces ethical scrutiny as well. This review aims to map academic research on salmon farming, analysing how studies address themes such as environmental impacts, socio-economic consequences, industrial profitability, and regulatory frameworks. We will search for relevant records from The Lens bibliographic meta-database using a tried-and-tested search strategy. We will then systematically screen records at title and abstract level and full text level according to a set of predefined inclusion criteria. Following this, we will systematically extract and code metadata, including geographical focus, study objectives and design, and funding sources. Visualisation tools, such as heat maps and interactive atlases, will illustrate research distribution and highlight gaps in the literature. The project will provide a comprehensive overview that will inform future systematic reviews and primary research, particularly in underexplored areas. This scoping review thus offers a foundation for a critical assessment of the research literature on salmon farming and its role in global food systems, social and ecological impacts, and the effectiveness of regulatory practices.

title: 157.Withdrawn: Comparative efficacy of an antimicrobial liquid bandage and antibiotic aerosol for bovine digital dermatitis treatment.
abstract: Withdrawal:https://www.cabidigitallibrary.org/doi/10.31220/agriRxiv.2024.00284-w

title: 97.Withdrawal Statement
abstract: This is to confirm that the preprint"Comparative efficacy of an antimicrobial liquid bandage and antibiotic aerosol for bovine digital dermatitis treatment"has been withdrawn.

title: 145.Fungicide Efficacy and Climate Impact on Wheat Black Point: Experimental and Computational Insights.
abstract: The preprint "Fungicide Efficacy and Climate Impact on Wheat Black Point: Experimental and Computational Insights" has been withdrawn.

title: 158.Effectiveness of policy interventions that have been implemented to increase agricultural productivity in Latin American and Caribbean regions: a systematic review protocol.
abstract: The study proposed in this protocol aims to systematically review the literature on agricultural productivity interventions in Latin America and the Caribbean in the last 10 years. This review encompasses a broad range of agricultural productivity policies, and restricts study inclusion criteria to rigorous impact evaluations and empirical quantitative studies. The proposed review is comprehensive in terms of the diversity of policies considered, exhaustive in terms of the databases that will be searched, and ambitious in terms of the volume of studies to be assessed, while maintaining a high standard of evidence.

title: 159.What Are the factors behind emerging zoonotic diseases associated with agrifood systems? A systematic map protocol.
abstract: Background: Emerging zoonotic diseases (hereafter called zoonoses) pose significant global threats to human health and wellbeing. An estimated 60 percent of known infectious diseases are zoonotic in origin and over the past decade, approximately 75% of those identified have originated in animals. Each year, zoonoses are responsible for 2.5 billion cases of human illness and 2.7 million human deaths worldwide. During the COVID pandemic, there were many discussions amongst UK government departments on what to do differently to prevent such pandemics in the future. Initially the discussion was focused on human health, however the Foreign, Commonwealth, and Development Office (FCDO) Food and Agriculture advisors recognised that many of the drivers of emerging zoonotic diseases were linked to agrifood systems and interactions between humans and livestock, including via livestock/wildlife (peri-domestic) contacts. Land use change and ecosystem degradation combined with rising human populations have amplified interactions between humans and animals. This, exacerbated by climate change and constant changes in socio-economics, when the distribution of wealth changes for different socio-demographic groups, increases the risk of zoonotic disease emergence. However, the specific causes of emergence of zoonotic diseases in the context of agrifood systems are less clear. Therefore, a systematic map was commissioned in order to address the emergence of zoonoses.

title: 160.Global opportunities and challenges to the uptake of biopesticides: an evidence map.
abstract: Background: Pesticides play a crucial role in agriculture by protecting crops, but they can harm human health and the environment by contaminating soil, water, and non-target species, reducing biodiversity. Global pesticide use has grown significantly, increasing by 30% per hectare between 2002 and 2018. There is an urgent need to reduce reliance on hazardous pesticides due to their severe negative impacts. Biopesticides, which are derived from natural sources (microbes, plants, etc.), are increasingly recognized as a safer alternative, as they can reduce pesticide poisoning and protect biodiversity. Despite growing global interest, their usage is limited compared to synthetic pesticides, with most use occurring in industrialized nations or large-scale crops like sugarcane or soybeans. For biopesticides to be successfully adopted by farmers, the process must transition from research and regulatory approval to practical education, market access, and support. Overcoming these barriers ensures farmers use biopesticides effectively in integrated pest management (IPM). This review arises from discussions between the Juno Evidence Alliance and the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO). The systematic mapping aims to describe the existing research on the barriers and facilitators to biopesticide use. Methods: The review will use bibliographic databases and grey literature to search for relevant studies published between 2016-2024. The search strategy includes keywords related to biopesticides and barriers/facilitators to their use. Screening criteria focus on studies about biopesticides, contextual challenges, and facilitators post-2016. A detailed coding scheme will extract data on geographic coverage, stakeholders, types of biopesticides, and the barriers/facilitators identified in each study. The synthesis will use visual tools like heat maps and geographical plots to display evidence on barriers and facilitators across various contexts and stages of biopesticide development. Gaps and well-researched areas will be identified to guide future research.

title: 161.How do crop varieties developed through different breeding methods perform in field in terms of yield and biotic and abiotic stress? A systematic review protocol.
abstract: Background: Despite Nepal's considerable progress towards sustainable development goals in recent years, much more needs to be done to address the key development challenges. Agriculture plays an indispensable role in Nepal's development trajectory, but Nepal faces complex challenges in its agricultural landscape. Addressing these challenges requires a coordinated effort and the use of robust scientific evidence to support decision making - knowledge on effectiveness of crop varieties will help to direct support and resources where they are needed most. Despite heavy investment in seed technology, benefits to crop productivity and farmer income have been limited. Changing weather patterns and an overreliance on imported crops have led to a potentially fragile system. Previous work has demonstrated a sizable evidence base on the yields of various crops produced through different plant breeding methods. There is therefore a need for an analysis of the effectiveness of these methodological approaches. Methods: This systematic review follows on from a recent systematic map that collated the literature from Nepal on crop yields and stress tolerance for different breeding methods. Briefly, this map searched for evidence across a suite of bibliographic databases and grey literature resources using a tried-and-tested search strategy. Potentially relevant records were screened against a set ofa priori, explicit eligibility criteria, ensuring consistency in application prior to use. Relevant records proceeded to meta-data extraction and coding, followed by visualisation and narrative description of the evidence base as a whole. Here, we describe the planned process by which these studies will be further subsetted to identify a consistent body of quantitative evidence relating to the impacts of crop breeding methods on yield, where those data are provided. We outline our plans for critically appraising the validity of these studies, focusing on critical risks of bias, including developing a robust appraisal tool and demonstrating consistency in its application. We then describe the plans for extraction of full data from included studies, and for meta-analysis and interpretation of these data.

title: 162.Prediction of regional heat stress risk for grazing dairy cows in a changing climate.
abstract: Context: For dairy cows housed indoors, ambient temperature and humidity are key drivers of heat stress, but for cows kept outdoors, solar radiation and wind speed are also important. Aim: We aimed to determine whether climate-driven changes in these variables affect heat stress risk where cows are outdoors during summer and shoulder seasons, particularly pasture-based farming systems such as New Zealand. Methods: Using daily climate projection data from 2006 to 2098, peak daily values of the temperature-humidity index (THI) of Thom (1959), and the grazing heat load index (GHLI) of Bryant et al. (2022) were calculated and used to map predicted changes in the annual (June to May) number of days with heat stress risk and the annual accumulated heat stress "load" (the sum of effective degrees C above the threshold) for dairy production regions of New Zealand. Key results: The results illustrated the limitations of using THI in the context of outdoor use, where solar radiation and wind speed are shown to be more important than humidity. The GHLI predicted that the risk of heat stress is already high in the Waikato (69 days), Bay of Plenty (69 days) and Canterbury (80 days) regions in the 2020s. Canterbury was also notable for having high heat stress load within day compared with other regions (i.e., heat stress days were particularly intense), attributable to the combined effect of high temperatures, clear skies and low wind speeds. Conclusions: According to climate projections, regions already experiencing high numbers of heat stress risk days and heat stress load in the 2020s will experience the greatest increases in heat stress risk to the 2050s. However, dramatic increases in the number of heat stress days are not anticipated. Implications: This allows research and development to focus on mitigation practices in these regions where dairy farming systems must adapt to a changing climate. Mitigation strategies may include provision of shade, access to sprinklers, genetic selection for heat stress resilience, modifying feeding regimes to reduce heat load, or development of new solutions and technologies.

title: 163.Enhancing quality of dairy cattle research through adequate power analysis.
abstract: Animal scientists use controlled experiments to test hypotheses and evaluate treatment effects within populations. Due to the impracticality of studying entire populations, representative samples are necessary. Assessing statistical power is a crucial step in designing robust experiments. However, many published articles in dairy science lack adequate power analysis, raising concerns about the applicability of findings. An analysis of trends from 1995 to 2023 based on publications in the "Production: Animal Nutrition" section of the Journal of Dairy Science reveals that only 4.73% of 4,376 articles reported power analysis. Additionally, 59% of papers that conducted power analysis did not report the tools used. With the large variability among the tools being used, and the predominant tool, SAS, being non-open access, there is a need to standardize power analysis with an open-source tool. To address this gap, we developed the pwr4exp R package, an open-source tool that provides comprehensive model-oriented power analysis tailored for dairy science research. This review discusses key experimental designs for performing power analysis using the pwr4exp R package. Developed based on linear mixed model inference, pwr4exp was validated by comparing with SAS procedures for completely randomized, randomized complete block, Latin Square, split-plot, or split-split-plot designs. It emphasizes the importance of model specification for downstream statistical analysis at the design and planning phase of an experiment and allows for precise power calculations for main effects, interactions, and contrasts in animal studies. Despite its advantages, pwr4exp in the current version has its limitations, such as the inability to analyze non-normal response variables. This paper reviews the theoretical foundation behind model-oriented power analysis and provides practical guidelines for standardizing power analysis in R, with examples of various experimental designs relevant in animal research.

title: 164.Can grain P concentration be used as an indicator of fertilizer requirements in winter wheat?
abstract: Available phosphorus (P) management is a continuous task in wheat-based systems of the UK, primarily to balance applying enough P to support high yields while avoiding unnecessary costs and damaging losses to the environment by applying too much. The widely used soil Olsen P method with corresponding threshold values is well established, has a known uncertainty interval around the 95% confidence interval, but the response can vary on some specific soil types. Therefore, grain P concentration with a corresponding threshold value of 0.32% has been proposed as a new method for P management. We used data from a long-term experiment called the Exhaustion Land experiment on the Rothamsted Farm in southeast England, to investigate the relations between winter wheat grain yield, grain P concentration, and Olsen P values in winter wheat over the last 32 years. Our results show that maximum grain P concentrations in high yielding years are much lower than in low yielding years, indicating a dilution effect through high assimilate transfer to grains. We could not confirm a lower threshold of 0.32% grain P as an indicator of crop P deficiency at high yields, in our trial the value was closer to 0.24% grain P. The Olsen P test at our site was a good indicator of P response, and the Olsen P threshold value of 20 mg P kg-1was sufficient to support the highest yields of winter wheat. We propose that P recommendations for cereals should be based on soil Olsen P values, possibly supported by better estimation of P exports based on grain analysis. Further, evaluation of the suitability of grain P concentration as a tool for P fertilizer management in cereal based systems would require more research. In the future, the existing Olsen P index classes in the current UK Nutrient Management Guide ('RB209') should be reviewed to possibly increase P fertilizer use efficiency and reduce P losses to the environment whilst maintaining current production levels.

title: 165.Optimization of sampling design for soil total organic carbon assessment in the precision agriculture framework: impact of different variogram models and potentiality of geophysical covariate information.
abstract: Assessing soil organic carbon (SOC) at the field scale is crucial for effective environmental and agronomic management, especially within the precision agriculture framework. This enables the implementation of strategies to enhance soil quality, increase carbon sequestration, and improve crop yields. However, the process of sampling and assessing SOC is resource-intensive, demanding both in time and labour. Methods for minimizing information loss while reducing the sampling scheme, such as spatial simulated annealing (SSI), are particularly valuable in the scope of SOC assessment, especially when faced with budget constraints. Within the structure of the SSI method, two critical components have been identified: i) the selection of highly informative covariates for the primary variable (SOC); ii) the selection of an appropriate variogram model for spatial variability assessment. Covariates strongly correlated with SOC, along with a well-performing model, can significantly enhance the efficiency of the sampling scheme reduction process. The selected covariates leverage indirect information obtained from ground penetrating radar (GPR) that can be collected at a higher spatial density compared to SOC data. We conducted this study using data from a field experiment, which included 71 georeferenced sampling locations. Through a stepwise approach, we progressively reduced the number of sampling points to 10, 15, and 20 observations. Utilizing SSI, we refined the sampling scheme according to two distinct variogram models: the spherical and Gaussian-Matérn models. This process allowed us to identify the optimal variogram model, which has a key role in maximizing the reduction of redundant points while preserving those with valuable information. Our findings underlined also the significance of covariates in regression-kriging, particularly when employing the spherical model, to predict the points excluded from the SOC sampling scheme.

title: 166.A framework to assess environmental outcomes of landscape-scale agricultural transition scenarios.
abstract: The United States (U.S.) Corn Belt leads North America in row crop production, yet this high productivity comes at an environmental cost in terms of nitrate loss, soil erosion, and greenhouse gas emissions. In this study, we focus on the Upper Mississippi River basin within the U.S. Corn Belt, which represents a landscape scale for agricultural transformation. We outline a methodological framework to assess a suite of environmental outcomes associated with the transition from summer annual maize/soybean systems to incorporation of continuous living cover systems. We use and expand publicly available tools alongside empirical data to assess nitrate loss, soil erosion, and greenhouse gas emissions for four potential agricultural transition scenarios in the region. We consider the following four scenarios: incorporating (1) winter annual cover crops or (2) winter annual oilseeds into 50% of maize and soybean hectares in the region, or converting 50% of marginally productive maize and soybean hectares to (3) agroforestry or (4) pastured livestock systems. Our results indicate that all four systems are likely to reduce topsoil loss when compared to maize and soybean systems, and that the more transformative systems-agroforestry and pastured livestock - have the greatest potential to reduce nitrate loss. Yet, our results suggest that among these transitions, there are tradeoffs in environmental outcomes. For example, pastured livestock and winter annual oilseeds could potentially increase greenhouse gas emissions relative to maize/soybean systems. Our results illustrate that continuous living cover could improve environmental outcomes in the Upper Midwest, but there is tremendous uncertainty and variability surrounding those outcomes.

title: 167.A new method for calculating the food self-sufficiency ratio: supply-side food self-sufficiency ratio.
abstract: Background: The conventional formula for calculating food self-sufficiency cannot cover all the food we eat on a daily basis, and the food self-sufficiency ratio (FSSR) of each country cannot be calculated. The conventional food self-sufficiency ratio (CFSSR) can only calculate the FSSRs of each country for grains. To determine the actual state of food insecurity worldwide as accurately as possible, a method for calculating the FSSR of each country for all the foods we eat on a daily basis is needed. To address this situation, this study proposes the supply-side food self-sufficiency ratio (SSFSSR), which can be used to systematically calculate the self-sufficiency ratio of all foods in all countries/regions. Results: We compared the results of both calculations under the same conditions and used the same data to determine whether the CFSSR or the SSFSSR is a more suitable method for obtaining basic information and formulating measures of global food security. The results showed that the SSFSSR has advantages and practicality over the CFSSR. The SSFSSR can calculate self-sufficiency ratios for all foods in all countries/regions of the world, and the figures for various statistical tests are better. The food that is the subject of the calculation in the SSFSSR formula is the entire supply from production, distribution, storage, and consumption, excluding duplication in the calculation, and includes primary products required to produce secondary products, such as livestock products and edible oils. The study also highlighted the value of reducing the amount of primary products used to produce secondary products such as livestock and edible oils, thereby lowering the primary product conversion rate (PPCR). Conclusion: This study used actual data to estimate the SSFSSR for each country/region to demonstrate the applicability of this method and that lowering the PPCR would lead to an increase in the food self-sufficiency ratio. To further refine this methodology, we find that the most important tasks for the future are to collect more reliable data on calories per weight for a large number of foods, expand the number of types covered by more reliable PPCRs, and analyze those data.

title: 168.Unoxygenated Kratky systems are a viable alternative to active deep water culture approaches.
abstract: In deep water culture (DWC) systems plants are suspended with their roots immersed in a tank of nutrient solution (Resh 2022) which is typically oxygenated and regularly adjusted for parameters such as pH and electrical conductivity (EC). Kratky systems are a simplified form of DWC in which the water level is allowed to drop, and additional oxygen inputs are not provided. Kratky systems have potential to increase the accessibility of food production. It was unknown if Kratky systems would be improved by additional oxygen or how their production compares to that of more intensive DWC approaches. We found that Kratky systems did not produce improved yields across three varieties of lettuce when dissolved oxygen was supplied through an air stone. We also found that Kratky systems produced yields and chlorophyll content in lettuce plants to the same level as DWC systems managed intensively as is often done commercially. Our findings support Kratky systems as a viable alternative to more intensive DWC approaches.

title: 169.Reflectance analysis of vegetative development of soy irrigated with slaughterhouse-treated effluent.
abstract: The link between wastewater reuse and sustainable agriculture emphasizes the significance of embracing innovative methods and technologies. Computer vision and digital image techniques, when combined with existing approaches such as vegetation indices and chlorophyll analysis, emerge as powerful instruments for plant nutritional monitoring and growth. The objective of this study was to analyze, by reflectance, the vegetative development of soybeans irrigated with treated slaughterhouse effluent. Also, the minor objectives were to (i) monitor soybean development using active and passive optical sensors by determining vegetative indices, and (ii) develop an algorithm for image segmentation and calculation of vegetation indices. This study was performed at an experimental area annex to a slaughterhouse at Pirassununga-Brazil. The effluent was treated and used to irrigate soybeans with concentrations of 0, 25, 50, 75, and 100% under the presence or absence of inoculation. Data was collected with a digital camera, a chlorophyll meter, and a GreenSeeker during its vegetative development. A Python script was developed to extract the vegetation indices from the images. The indices investigated in this study presented different behaviors throughout the soybean vegetative development, with significative differences (p<0.05) in the days after sowing, treatment, inoculation, and their interaction. This represents the first documented attempt to analyze vegetation indices obtained from images taken using a digital camera at a field scale of a crop irrigated with treated wastewater.

title: 170.RGB image-based detection of nutrient deficiencies in barley by deep learning methods.
abstract: Two or four spring barley genotypes, respectively, were cultivated under single-nutrient-deficient conditions of essential mineral nutrients in four experimental systems: (i) a hydroponic system in greenhouse (HyPo), (ii) a pot experiment in soil in greenhouse (SoPo), (iii) a Mini-Plot experiment under field-like conditions (MiPlo), and (iv) a long-term fertilizer field experiment (Diko). Shoot phenotypes were recorded using a Huawei P20 smartphone camera, thus generating large-scale datasets of annotated RGB images that were analyzed with Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)-based deep learning (DL) models. Plant samples were collected to determine the nutritional status of the plant. For an initial assessment of the suitability of the experimental systems, we present plant morphological data and nutrient concentrations as well as five comprehensive RGB datasets raised from the conducted experiments and respective CNN model prediction accuracies by experiment and treatment. Investigated target nutrients of deficiency treatments were: N, P and K across all experiments, in MiPlo additionally S and B, in SoPo and HyPo, furthermore, Mn, Zn, Mo and Cu, and only in Hypo Ca, Mg and Fe. Target nutrient concentrations in plants grown under deficiency treatments were reduced across all experiments, but did not always result in a reduced biomass. In particular, even though S, B and Mo deficiency treatments could be detected by the CNN model, the evaluated plant parameters hardly indicated the respective deficiencies. The achieved average prediction accuracies from RGB datasets including all investigated genotypes and nutrient treatments per experiment were 38.52% in HyPo, 61.78% in SoPo, 70.3% in MiPlo and 94.5% in Diko, respectively. The achieved average prediction accuracies from standardized RGB datasets, including only those genotypes and nutrient treatments (N, P and K) that were investigated across all experiments, were 48.8% in HyPo, 88.8% in SoPo, 85.5% in MiPlo and 82.4% in Diko, respectively, indicating that soil-based experiments are more suitable for acquisition of RGB datasets for CNN-based nutrient deficiency detection than experiments in nutrient solutions. The results further highlight the potential of an RGB-based deep learning approach for an element-specific non-invasive on-site and real-time diagnosis of nutrient deficiencies in crop plants.

title: 171.Cultivating sustainable agriculture: traditional wisdom in Balinese rice farming.
abstract: Rice farming in Bali, particularly within theSubakorganization, blends modern practices with indigenous wisdom across 779 hectares of rice land. This paper explores the integration of local culture in Balinese rice farming, analyzing its implementation, factors influencing preservation, and alignment with ideal expectations. Drawing on cultural rituals such asTutug Kambuhan,Nangluk Merana,Mebiukukung, andSarin Taun, we highlight the significance ofTri Hita Karanaa philosophy emphasizing harmonious relationships with divinity, humanity, and the environment. Despite generational shifts and challenges, farmers uphold cultural practices, albeit with discrepancies between ideal and actual conditions. Recommendations include university collaborations, organic farming promotion, and land suitability mapping for sustainable agricultural development.

title: 172.Genomic prediction of maize tassel traits through LiDAR point cloud segmentation and machine learning phenotyping.
abstract: The development of automated, high-throughput, and accurate measurement of plant phenotypes across different genotypes, environments, and field conditions is essential to overcoming current phenotyping bottlenecks. This study aimed to create a novel phenotyping platform using 3D LiDAR technology to measure key maize tassel traits (compactness, length, and width) in real field conditions. We utilized a high-throughput Pegasus Backpack LiDAR device for field walk scanning, capturing 3D point clouds of individual plants. Advanced machine learning algorithms, including K-means clustering and Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (DBSCAN), were employed to segment individual maize plants and extract tassel traits from the dense canopy. Our approach successfully segmented and phenotyped 13,190 individual plants across diverse maize genetic backgrounds, significantly increasing the number of data points per genotype, with a median of 28 plants segmented per plot. We used high-resolution phenotypic data in genome-wide association studies to pinpoint specific gene associated markers and to optimize genomic prediction models for inferring the genetic architecture of tassel traits. This method not only enhances the accuracy of trait measurement but also holds broader implications for other crops, potentially accelerating the development of high-yielding, resilient varieties. The results pave the way for precision breeding, facilitating the development of new varieties better suited to modern agricultural challenges, ultimately supporting global food security and sustainability.

title: 174.Balancing nets and lives: a socio-ecological analysis of sustainable fisheries in the gulf of Mannar.
abstract: The Gulf of Mannar, a UNESCO World Biosphere Reserve, faces severe overfishing and habitat degradation threats. In this study, we investigate the pivotal role of ecosystem services in sustaining local livelihoods and overall well-being. By conducting a comprehensive survey of 480 respondents across two districts, we gathered extensive data on demographics, livelihoods, fishing practices, reliance on ecosystem services, and community management participation. The analysis reveals a critical dependence on the Gulf's resources (income, food security, traditions) with gender disparities (men fish, women in pre/post-harvest), but fishing is only allowed in the 10 km buffer zone (not the core zone). The findings emphasize the promise of community-based strategies, such as Marine Protected Areas and reviving co-management committees, for achieving sustainable fisheries management. However, we also identify gaps, including the need for more nuanced well-being indicators and improved models for community management participation. To address these challenges, we advocate for sustainable fishing practices, tackling social inequities, especially gender disparities in resource access and decision-making, and investing in healthcare, education, and social safety nets for fishing communities. Promoting alternative livelihoods can alleviate pressure on fish stocks, and empowering local communities through capacity building and community-based management initiatives is crucial for ensuring the long-term sustainability of both the Gulf of Mannar ecosystem and the well-being of its dependent communities. This multifaceted approach holds significant promise for balancing ecological health with human prosperity.

title: 175.Water, wealth, and wellbeing: groundwater development's socioeconomic impact in Coimbatore district.
abstract: This study investigates the socioeconomic impacts of groundwater use in Coimbatore district, India, from 2013 to 2023, with a focus on disparities between rural and urban areas and the challenges faced by vulnerable groups. Employing a multifaceted approach, it includes time series analysis of groundwater extraction rates and GIS mapping of borewells to explore spatial disparities in groundwater dependence. The research examines the correlations between groundwater levels and socioeconomic indicators such as income, poverty rates, and agricultural employment patterns, using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient. By identifying trends and spatial variations, the study aims to inform sustainable water management policies and promote responsible consumption and production practices, ensuring long-term water security for the Coimbatore district.

title: 176.Assessing the impact of agrifood systems interventions on resilience - a protocol for a rapid evidence assessment.
abstract: While significant efforts have been done to homogenise the definition of resilience and to build frameworks for resilience measurement (Frankenbergeret al., 2014; United Nations, 2020), a common understanding of interventions that contribute to build resilience and their effectiveness is missing. This hinders the comprehension of underlying theories of change and the assessment of programme (cost-) effectiveness. FAO's efforts to strengthen resilience are embedded in the UN Humanitarian Response Plans and Sustainable Development Cooperation Frameworks. FAO assists the most food insecure and vulnerable communities to build their resilience to shocks and stresses and ensure long-term food security and nutrition. Yet, these are often fragile environments with increasingly frequent and intense shocks and stresses, and local contexts strongly determine the success or failure of resilience-enhancing initiatives and ad-hoc responses. The traditional twin-track approach of FAO focused on emergencies response and recovery and development does not always address the underlying causes of protracted crises (e.g., conflict and structural inequalities) and may struggle to secure necessary resources to support long-term resilience, as donors may prioritize short-term relief (Gerber, 2016). Interventions targeting agrifood systems and aiming to build resilience have been insufficiently researched, highlighting a gap in defining of what constitutes an "intervention for resilience" and in understanding the impact of different types of intervention for resilience (Barrettet al., 2021). In particular, anecdotes from the field underscore the potential for high effectiveness in appropriate sequencing and combination of interventions for building resilience, but this is supported by very limited evidence. There is a need to explore (1) which types of and sets of interventions are most suitable and (cost-) effective for resilience, by differentiating sub-national contexts, as well as exposure to various shocks and stresses; (2) which enabling conditions are determinant for the effectiveness of the interventions. An answer to such questions should provide FAO with a menu of "interventions for resilience" that can be tailored to the different contexts, to support country level resilience programming.

title: 177.Genetic architecture of ideotype-related traits in middle American beans through single trait, multi-trait and epistatic genome-wide analyses.
abstract: Common bean is one of the major legume crops for direct human consumption. The genetic improvement of common bean is a primary approach to increase crop adaptability to climate change conditions while maintaining productivity. A diverse panel of middle American beans was evaluated over three growing seasons (2021, 2022 and 2023) for agronomic traits considered in the crop ideotype such as flowering, maturity, pigment content, lodging, and yield. A study of the genetic regions controlling trait variation was carried out using single-trait and simultaneous (joint) multi-trait GWAS approaches. Additionally, genome-wide epistatic interactions were also analyzed. Several previously reported and novel regions were identified as significant for individual traits in the single and multi-year analyses with varying percentages of phenotypic variance explained (11 - 49%). In the single-trait multi-year analyses, marlers detected for lodging showed the highest average of percentage of variance explained (49%) followed by the others traits with percentages between 11 and 19%. For yield, new loci were found with estimated effects between -96.19 to 90.96 Kg/Ha. In the multi-trait analyses, a locus on Pv02 and another on Pv04 were identified to have interaction effects on flowering and yield. On Pv0Pv04, a locus showed a common effect between lodging and maturity, characterized by several SNPs. Significant epistatic interactions were found along different chromosomes for all the evaluated traits, with some loci having interactions with multiple regions. In flowering, an interaction between loci on Pv01 and Pv04 explained up to 10.5% of the phenotypic variation, followed by interactions between Pv06 and Pv10 for chlorophyll b and between Pv03 and Pv08 for yield explaining around 6% of the trait variation. Multiple transcription factors were identified as candidate genes, particularly in the pairs of combinations of epistatic effects. Based on the homology analyses of the candidate genes, several showed potential roles in the genetic control of the agronomic traits, particularly for flowering, maturity, and yield. Our results demonstrate the applicability of various approaches for common bean and show a comprehensive and expanded panorama of the genetic basis of agronomic traits. The results provide new resources for crop improvement that can be leveraged in multiple approaches such as selection, modelling and predicting crop performance and genetic gain.

title: 178.Assessment of contextually relevant nutrition-sensitive interventions that can effectively and sustainably address food security and support the achievement of nutrition security by 2030.
abstract: Globally, 9.2% or 735 million people are chronically hungry and 2.2 billion are food insecure, and most of these populations reside in countries across Southern Asia and Eastern and Middle Africa (FAO, 2023c). Within lower-middle income countries (LMICs), rural and peri-urban populations suffer from prolonged and seasonal periods of food insecurity, and lack consistent access to diverse, safe, and nutrient-rich foods (FAO, 2023c). Meanwhile, an estimated 20% of the global mortality are attributed to poor diet quality, i.e., diets low in whole grains, vegetables and fruits, and high sodium and sugar (Afshin et al., 2019). One in two pre-school aged children and two out three women of reproductive age have at least one micronutrient deficiency (Stevens et al., 2022). Multiple forms of malnutrition, such as hunger, food insecurity, and, nutrient inadequacy, which coexist within households and communities, pose large health and economic burdens for countries. Chronic exposure to food insecurity at different life stages has long-term consequences on many forms of malnutrition. Clinical, epidemiology, and epigenetic studies have illustrated that early life undernutrition and prolonged exposure to hunger increases the risk of developing obesity and diabetes later in life (Chandak et al., 2017; Popkin et al., 2020; Uauy et al., 2011). Women and young children form a more significant proportion of hungry people globally and face a higher likelihood of developing multiple forms of malnutrition at critical stages throughout their lives (FAO et. al, 2023). Women who are undernourished and experience excess maternal weight gain during pregnancy have higher levels of gestational diabetes, increasing the risk for adverse maternal and child nutritional outcomes (Victoria et al. 2008). In areas with poor market access, smallholder farmers' diets that are largely shaped by what they produce, and in peri-urban and urban areas the availability of low-cost, ultra-processed foods is contributing to increased consumption of unhealthy consumption.
